The guide therefore ranks medal spending by long-term account value instead of by what is merely available in the current event shop rotation. Relevant site data fits that framing because Medals feed several different event-shop branches at once: Event Relics, Event Songs, Event Themes, currency exchanges, and permanent bot progression.

title: Medals Guide Past Relics
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Medals Guide Past Relics mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic medal-spending summary outside the medals guide, a current-event inventory readout, or a weekly reward table.
content: Medals Guide Past Relics. High-value past relics come first whenever a rerun shop offers one that meaningfully improves the account, with Lab Speed and coin relics called out as the clearest priorities. Site data says Event Relics are separate store purchases from current-event medal thresholds, sold through the shop at 200-medal and 500-medal price points rather than through Event Relic Progress. That distinction matters because missing a strong past relic is not the same as delaying a repeatable currency purchase. If the relic is genuinely high impact, the guide treats it as the first medal claim on the budget.

title: Medals Guide Songs and Themes
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Medals Guide Songs and Themes mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic medal-spending summary outside the medals guide, a current-event inventory readout, or a weekly reward table.
content: Medals Guide Songs and Themes. Songs and themes come next because their passive coin value stacks permanently even though each individual bonus looks small. Site data says there are 3 Event Songs, each costing 200 medals and granting +0.6% coin bonus, while Event Themes rotate by event and cost 150 medals for one tower theme plus 250 medals for one background theme. That means buying both event themes in a rotation costs 400 medals, while songs build a separate permanent coin-bonus pool that never rotates away once purchased. Theme data also shows that owned tower themes add +0.4% passive coin bonus each and owned background themes add +0.8% each, so the guide is prioritizing long-term stacking rather than one-time cosmetics for appearance alone.

title: Medals Guide Stones and Gems
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Medals Guide Stones and Gems mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic medal-spending summary outside the medals guide, a current-event inventory readout, or a weekly reward table.
content: Medals Guide Stones and Gems. Stone packs are the next recommendation, but only in moderation. The guide caps them at about one or two purchases because the medal exchange ladder rises fast and the value decays immediately after the early buys. Site data says Event Shop Currency Purchases give either 150 gems, 15 stones, or 250 shards, with the shared medal ladder increasing through 40, 65, 90, 130, 175, 230, and 380 medals. Gems are treated much more strictly. The guide only allows a gem purchase before all five labs are unlocked, and even then usually only a single pack when it meaningfully speeds up Lab slot progress. After all five labs are unlocked, the guide treats medal-bought gems as inefficient because Gems are easier to source elsewhere while Medals are still competing with stronger event-store permanents.

title: Medals Guide Bot Progression
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Medals Guide Bot Progression mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic medal-spending summary outside the medals guide, a current-event inventory readout, or a weekly reward table.
content: Medals Guide Bot Progression. Bots come after the higher-value permanent shop targets, and the guide explicitly rejects unlocking all four immediately just because the roster is visible in the store. The core rule is to unlock a bot, invest into the upgrades that actually make it work, and only then move to the next bot instead of spreading medals across several weak low-level bots. Site data supports that approach because bot unlock costs escalate from 150 to 300 to 600 to 900 medals, while all bot stat upgrades use the same shared medal ladder from 100 up to 860 by level 20. The guide also warns against cooldown upgrades unless the player understands the synchronization tradeoffs. Bot Respec exists, but it costs 300 Gems once per event, so careless cooldown investment is still expensive to clean up.

title: Medals Guide Coin Bot Priorities
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Medals Guide Coin Bot Priorities mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic medal-spending summary outside the medals guide, a current-event inventory readout, or a weekly reward table.
content: Medals Guide Coin Bot Priorities. Coin Bot is the first bot priority. The guide recommends working Range and Bonus first, keeping Range only a couple of levels ahead of Bonus, and leaving Cooldown alone unless there is a specific GT or BH sync target. Site data maps the permanent event-shop Golden Bot alias back to Coin Bot and shows its upgrade families as Duration, Cooldown, Bonus, and Range. The guide intentionally narrows that full stat set down to the upgrades that matter most for actual early value. Cooldown is treated as low-value without a synchronization plan because a mistimed Coin Bot rarely improves much on its own. The guide does not want medals tied up in cooldown changes that fail to line up with Golden Tower or Black Hole windows. The next bot only starts when Coin Bot Range and Bonus are either maxed or at least well developed, because a partly built Coin Bot already contributes more than a newly unlocked but weak follow-up bot.

title: Medals Guide Later Bot Priorities
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Medals Guide Later Bot Priorities mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic medal-spending summary outside the medals guide, a current-event inventory readout, or a weekly reward table.
content: Medals Guide Later Bot Priorities. Amplify Bot: Second bot priority after Coin Bot. Upgrade Range first because widening the area improves the chance bosses pass through it. Add Bonus after Range is well developed so the damage multiplier becomes worth the activation window. Thunder Bot: Third bot priority. Treat it as a crowd-control tool that needs heavy investment before it becomes reliably useful. A low-level Thunder Bot can create problems for some builds, so the guide would rather delay it than spread medals too thinly. Flame Bot: Last bot priority. Only invest once the other bots are maxed or already properly levelled. The guide treats Flame Bot as cleanup work, not as an early medal sink that should compete with stronger permanent gains.

title: Orb Devo Guide Overview
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orb Devo Guide Overview mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo summary outside the Orb Devo guide, a live tracker state, or a single stat formula page.
content: Orb Devo Guide Overview. Orb Devo is one branch inside the broader devo family, where players intentionally leave some kill-related stats underlevelled so enemies die only during the right multiplier window instead of leaking value all run long. The guide frames Orb Devo as an eHP hoarding strategy built around synchronized Black Hole and Golden Tower activations, with Orbs handling the cash-out once the stack is positioned correctly. Relevant site data matches that framing because Orb Devo depends on exact overlap between Ultimate Weapon timing, Tower Range, Extra Orb positioning, Black Hole pickup coverage, and controlled workshop rows that would otherwise clear enemies too early.

title: Orb Devo Guide Requirements
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orb Devo Guide Requirements mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo summary outside the Orb Devo guide, a live tracker state, or a single stat formula page.
content: Orb Devo Guide Requirements. The hard opener is Black Hole and Golden Tower in sync, with Multiverse Nexus allowed as a temporary bridge if the account does not have natural sync yet. The guide wants Extra Orb unlocked, Extra Orb Adjuster researched, Tower Range pushed to 69.5m during the run, and the Extra Orb card positioned at 60m so the Orb pass catches the Black Hole stack instead of clipping it too early. Black Hole size is expected to reach roughly 38m to 42m minimum so the full stack gets pulled, with more size preferred for reliable coverage. Shockwave size is tuned rather than maxed. The guide calls out about 1.4 for a non-Wall setup and about 1.65 to 1.75 if Wall is being used, because the goal is shuffling basics into trim positions instead of scattering the whole stack.

title: Orb Devo Guide Workshop Devo
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orb Devo Guide Workshop Devo mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo summary outside the Orb Devo guide, a live tracker state, or a single stat formula page.
content: Orb Devo Guide Workshop Devo. Attack rows left at zero: Attack Speed Multishot Chance Rapid Fire Chance Bounce Shot Chance Defense rows left at zero or tightly controlled: Thorn Damage stays at zero until trimmed up during the run Knockback Chance Orbs Shockwave Size stays at a tuned shuffle value instead of climbing freely Land Mine Chance Land Mine Radius Utility rows left at zero until the blender exit: Free Attack Upgrade Free Defense Upgrade Free Utility Upgrade Optional rows kept low for variant devo paths: Critical Chance for players extending damage devo variants Range at 30m base for alternate setups Land Mine Damage only for Land Mine Stun or Spotlight-driven land-mine offshoots

topic: Orb Devo Guide Cards and Support
title: Orb Devo Guide Cards and Support
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orb Devo Guide Cards and Support mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo summary outside the Orb Devo guide, a live tracker state, or a single stat formula page.
content: Orb Devo Guide Cards and Support. Required cards: Extra Orb Coins Critical Coin Cash Enemy Balance Health Extra Defense Economy cards: Wave Skip Wave Accelerator Defensive swaps: Regen when the tower is using Wall or Wormhole Redirector Recovery Package Chance when Wall is absent or Galaxy Compressor is being used Optional utility cards: Fortress for early-run stability Land Mine Stun once land-mine damage is no longer ruining the stack and a strong Land Mine Radius setup exists The guide strongly prefers maxed Black Hole Coin Bonus and Black Hole Damage, plus both Extra Extra Orb labs, because Orb Devo becomes much stronger once both the hold window and the payout window are mature. Death Wave and Spotlight are both treated as major power spikes rather than mandatory unlocks. Death Wave adds health, coins, and cells, while Spotlight adds another coin multiplier on the same kill window. A 25-second Black Hole duration with perk support is the key protector threshold named in the guide, because at max Black Hole Damage it makes protectors die in two cycles. Extra Black Hole, Garlic Thorns, lower synced cooldowns on Black Hole, Golden Tower, and Death Wave, Extra Orb Mastery, and a synced Coin Bot are all listed as meaningful upgrades once the base shell already works.
mechanics: Orb Devo Guide Cards and Support

title: Orb Devo Guide Run Plan
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orb Devo Guide Run Plan mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo summary outside the Orb Devo guide, a live tracker state, or a single stat formula page.
content: Orb Devo Guide Run Plan. The basic run loop is to hoard enemies, eHP tank the pile, then let synchronized Black Hole and Golden Tower pull the full screen inward so Orbs can cash it out inside the multiplier window. After the setup is stable, run cash goes mostly into survival: Enemy Attack Level Skip, Wall if available, Health, Regen when a Wall or Wormhole Redirector plan exists, Defense Absolute, and Defense %. Thorn Damage is micromanaged instead of freely upgraded. The guide wants basics trimmed because they are worth less than tanks, but it does not want Thorn Damage high enough to start breaking the real stack. Once survival is starting to fail, cash goes into the three Free Upgrade rows and the run exits into a normal blender finish instead of pretending the devo shell still has clean control.

title: Orb Devo Guide Perk Priorities
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orb Devo Guide Perk Priorities mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo summary outside the Orb Devo guide, a live tracker state, or a single stat formula page.
content: Orb Devo Guide Perk Priorities. Economy perk priorities: Perk Wave Requirement Coin Trade-Off Golden Tower Bonus Black Hole Duration Coins Extra Death Wave Cash Defensive perk priorities: Regen Trade-Off Regen Defense % Max HP Defense Absolute 50/50 Damage Trade-Off

title: Orb Devo Guide Survival Priorities
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orb Devo Guide Survival Priorities mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo summary outside the Orb Devo guide, a live tracker state, or a single stat formula page.
content: Orb Devo Guide Survival Priorities. Low lifetime coin survival: In Tier 1 and Tier 2 starts, Defense Absolute is the first real survival crutch and is pushed to about 1000 workshop levels before Health takes over Health is then pushed toward roughly 5000 so it can be cash-maxed in run Wormhole Redirector makes Regen matter later, but the guide warns that early Regen scaling is weak before very deep investment Lab survival goals: Defense % to level 23 so capped defense is reachable with an ancestral substat and strong perk support Death Wave Health Health lab to about level 50 Maxed Standard Perk Bonus Enemy Attack Level Skip support Early mid-game survival: Wormhole Redirector is treated as the default best survivability module once real module options exist High-rarity Defense % substats are prioritized Land Mine Radius becomes valuable late only when Land Mine Stun can lock enemies without ruining the stack Thorn Damage also helps reach later Wall-thorns breakpoints and extend the final blender phase

topic: Orb Devo Guide Protector and Thorns Control
title: Orb Devo Guide Protector and Thorns Control
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orb Devo Guide Protector and Thorns Control mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo summary outside the Orb Devo guide, a live tracker state, or a single stat formula page.
content: Orb Devo Guide Protector and Thorns Control. Protectors are the main named nuisance. The guide solves them by maxing Black Hole Damage and reaching the 25-second Black Hole duration threshold so two Black Hole cycles reliably finish them. Because bullet damage stays low, elites and bosses are often killed mostly by thorns and survival layers instead of by the tower projectile shell. The thorns-trimming rule is to start around 15% to 20% Thorn Damage before Wall, then raise it slowly between activations so basics are thinned without deleting too many tanks or scattering the pile. Shockwave naturally shuffles tanks backward in the stack, so Thorn Damage and Shockwave tuning are treated as one combined control problem rather than isolated upgrades.
mechanics: Orb Devo Guide Protector and Thorns Control

title: Orbless Guide Overview
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orbless Guide Overview mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic orbless one-liner, a live tracker state, or a single stat definition page.
content: Orbless Guide Overview. Orbless is a family of farming builds built around maximizing Spotlight kills, not one fixed recipe. The shared goal is to kill inside overlapping Spotlight, Golden Tower, and Black Hole bonus windows while minimizing spillage outside those zones. The guide positions Orbless as the natural progression after synced blender and devo shells, because the account is mature enough to control both kill location and survival instead of accepting broad uncontrolled clears. Relevant site data matches that framing because Orbless depends on overlapping Ultimate Weapon coin bonuses, Spotlight coverage, Black Hole coverage, and tightly controlled workshop or module choices that would otherwise leak kills outside the preferred bonus window.

title: Orbless Guide Requirements
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orbless Guide Requirements mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic orbless one-liner, a live tracker state, or a single stat definition page.
content: Orbless Guide Requirements. The hard floor is a devo-style workshop that can still cash-max the needed battle stats in run, except for longer-term rows such as Rend Armor and Enemy Level Skip that are expected to lag behind full cash maxing. Perk support wants 4 options, 4 bans, Standard Perk Bonus 25, and Improve Trade-Off Perks 10 as the ideal shell. Auto Perk is explicitly rejected because Orbless often delays defensive or damage perks until the exact phase where they are needed. Synchronized Golden Tower and Black Hole with Extra Black Hole and more than 50% uptime is the real economy requirement. Permanent GT and BH are strongly preferred, GT Bonus wants to be at least 16x, and Black Hole Coin Bonus should already be maxed. Black Hole size must fully cover the tower range, with the guide calling out about 44m to 48m at 30m range and preferring more size when possible. Spotlight wants 3 beams, at least 40 degrees of angle, at least 20x bonus, maxed Spotlight Coin Bonus, and preferably a Spotlight Angle core substat. The SL4 warning is important: with 3 beams one beam is always aimed at a Black Hole, but with 4 beams you can create coverage gaps unless Spotlight Angle is already much higher, roughly 60 degrees or better.

title: Orbless Guide Survival Modes
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orbless Guide Survival Modes mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic orbless one-liner, a live tracker state, or a single stat definition page.
content: Orbless Guide Survival Modes. Wall survival shell: Wall is one of the three main survival branches and wants at least Wall Regen 10, Wall Thorns 11, plus enough Health, Health Regen, Wall Health, and Wall Fortification to actually survive long waves. The guide also calls out Standard Perk Bonus 25, Defense % 23, an ancestral Armor module with ancestral Defense %, and the Maxed Defense card as the mature support package behind a real wall-based Orbless build. If uptime is still weak early in the run, Thorns may need to stay devoed so enemies do not die to wall or thorn contact outside the intended Spotlight kill zone. Permanent Black Hole control: Permanent Black Hole prevents standard enemies from chipping the tower and lets the build tank bosses separately, but elites, especially vampires, can still be a problem if Wall is not also covering the run. The guide treats Black Hole Disable Ranged Enemies as absolutely required for this path because permanent BH is not enough if ranged enemies continue firing from inside the hole. Combining permanent BH with Wall is explicitly allowed and often stronger than relying on either system alone. Glass cannon juggling: Glass cannon is the third survival branch and leans on max Chrono Field to make conventional chip juggling manageable. That path still needs separate answers for rays and bosses, so the guide presents glass cannon as a specialist branch for towers whose stones and damage shell are already mature enough to carry it. The overall Orbless rule still holds: survival style and kill style can be mixed, so a tower can juggle conventional enemies while delegating bosses to Wall or another survival layer.

title: Orbless Guide Kill Methods
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orbless Guide Kill Methods mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic orbless one-liner, a live tracker state, or a single stat definition page.
content: Orbless Guide Kill Methods. Bullet Orbless: Bullet Orbless is the simplest entry point: make bullets kill at least 20 times faster inside Spotlight than outside it, then keep projectile behavior localized enough that conventional enemies only die in the beam. The guide names Damage / Meter, Rend Armor, Astral Deliverance, and minimal Bounce Shot Range as the main bullet tools. Astral Deliverance is the standout because higher-rarity bounce scaling localizes damage inside the Black Hole clump instead of spreading it across the screen. Astral Deliverance is expected to be mythic or better before it becomes truly effective. The raw guide calls out about 3.8x damage on the fourth bounce at legendary, 6.5x at mythic, and 10.5x at ancestral, with higher bounce substats also raising the average bounce count. Target Priority 2 is treated as nearly essential here. Using In Spotlight greatly reduces spillage compared with Closest targeting, which can cost a significant amount of coins per minute. Chain Lightning Orbless: Chain Lightning is presented as the second-easiest kill shell and usually extends bullet Orbless instead of replacing it from the first wave. The guide warns that Chain Lightning can be too aggressive at the start of a run, so the normal pattern is bullet Orbless first, then switching CL on after bullet-only killing starts to fade. Chain Lightning wants Shock unlocked, Shock Multiplier effectively maxed, Shock Chance around 10 or better, and CL damage held to about 596x or less until the player already understands the spillage breakpoints of the build. Spotlight Missiles Orbless: Spotlight Missiles is the classic Orbless method because it only targets enemies inside Spotlight, which naturally enforces the kill-zone rule instead of relying on projectile restraint alone. This path expects the Spotlight Missiles lab to be maxed, Smart Missiles to be unlocked, roughly 34x Smart Missiles damage at minimum, and both Missile Amp and Radius pushed high enough to support the beam kill zone. The guide explicitly allows max Radius because enemies outside Spotlight can survive the blast while still being tagged by Missile Amp, making them easier to finish when they rotate into Spotlight later. Other specialist kill shells: ILM+ or SLIME is acknowledged as another Orbless family member, but the guide treats it as a later specialist branch beyond its own scope. Land Mines are described as a support damage layer rather than a primary kill shell. They work best when Land Mine Radius is kept minimal, Land Mine Damage is maxed, and spillage is already low enough that mines spawn only in the preferred kill zone.

title: Orbless Guide Nice-to-Haves
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orbless Guide Nice-to-Haves mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic orbless one-liner, a live tracker state, or a single stat definition page.
content: Orbless Guide Nice-to-Haves. For lower-uptime builds, the guide specifically likes mythic-or-better Singularity Harness plus a synced Coin Bot. That setup can outperform Galaxy Compressor while uptime is still mediocre because it adds another multiplier window rather than only compressing cooldowns. Once GT and BH uptime is already high, roughly above 60%, the guide often prefers Galaxy Compressor instead because extra cooldown compression can push the build toward more permanent GT, BH, and Death Wave overlap than Singularity Harness can provide. Anti-Cube Portal is called out as a major Orbless spike and the raw guide claims ancestral ACP can extend the Orbless phase by roughly 1000 waves. Death Wave is another stacking multiplier and also supports wall-based builds through extra health. The guide prefers Death Wave synced to Golden Tower, wants the Death Wave coin lab maxed, and values Quantity most because the build wants to tag as many enemies as possible without overkilling outside Spotlight. Death Wave damage should stay controlled when possible because unlike Spotlight Missiles it kills indiscriminately and can create the same spillage problem Orbless is trying to solve.

title: Orbless Guide Run Phases
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orbless Guide Run Phases mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic orbless one-liner, a live tracker state, or a single stat definition page.
content: Orbless Guide Run Phases. Start of run: Remove damage cards and turn off damage Ultimate Weapons other than Death Wave. The tower is simply too strong early to avoid spillage, so the real priorities are perk setup, Enemy Level Skip progress, and maxing Death Wave health if that shell is being used. Perk choices in this phase prefer Perk Wave Requirement, coin perks, and the Spotlight perk while actively avoiding early damage perks. Optional Death Wave devo phase: Some towers gain more by briefly staying in a Death Wave focused devo phase after the first kill ring falls, especially if the account still has substantial GT or BH downtime. Higher-uptime towers can often skip this and dive directly into Orbless, but lower-uptime towers may earn more by letting Death Wave tag the full stack before tightening the kill zone. Initial Orbless phase: Battle upgrades usually stay untouched except for Enemy Level Skip until enemy density and HP naturally become high enough that enemies no longer die immediately outside Spotlight. This phase can last hundreds or thousands of waves, and the guide commonly delays most perk picks during it unless a defensive perk is required to keep the tower alive. Balancing upgrades: Once Orbless stops killing efficiently, the build starts carefully adding damage through selected battle upgrades, perks, or card swaps without tipping back into indiscriminate screen-wide kills. The guide treats this as the timer for the end of the Orbless shell: every extra damage lever extends kill power but also increases the risk of new spillage. Transitions and end state: An Orbless run can transition between multiple kill shells, such as bullet into SLM into CL, instead of ending the moment the first shell stops working. The real end arrives once damage upgrades, damage perks, and damage cards are already exhausted and income drops below the run average because kills are no longer fast enough to sustain respawns. At that point the build either ends for coin efficiency or exits into blender for cells.

title: Orbless Guide Workshop Setup
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orbless Guide Workshop Setup mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic orbless one-liner, a live tracker state, or a single stat definition page.
content: Orbless Guide Workshop Setup. The workshop foundation is still devo: leave Attack Speed, Range, Multishot Chance, Rapid Fire Chance, Bounce Shot Chance, Bounce Shot Range, Orbs, Land Mine Chance, Land Mine Radius, and Free Upgrades at zero. Crit Chance, Damage / Meter, Thorns, and Knockback can be optionally relaxed for lazier or more advanced variants. Bounce Shot Range staying at zero is especially important for bullet Orbless because the build wants bounce chains to stay inside the Black Hole clump instead of searching farther targets. Shockwave Size is tuned to about 1.35 in the raw guide so enemies are tagged by Anti-Cube Portal and basics are sifted below tanks for trimming without blowing the whole stack apart. Damage rows can still be levelled to reasonable long-term account breakpoints, with the guide giving one example shell of Damage around 5600 and Super Crit Multiplier around 100, but those values serve the later balancing phase rather than replacing devo control. The guide also wants at least two card presets: an early preset with damage cards removed and a late preset that adds those damage cards back in when the run is ready to spend them as a controlled upgrade lever.

title: Orbless Guide Module Choices
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orbless Guide Module Choices mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic orbless one-liner, a live tracker state, or a single stat definition page.
content: Orbless Guide Module Choices. Cannon modules: Astral Deliverance is the preferred Cannon module because bullet builds want the bounce damage ramp and glass-cannon juggling builds also benefit from the added bounce reach. The preferred substats are Bounce Shot, Multishot Targets, and crit-focused rolls. Attack Speed is explicitly devalued because dense enemy stacks make extra multishot targets more useful than faster firing. Death Penalty is rejected because it can kill enemies outside the Spotlight bonus zone. Armor modules: Anti-Cube Portal is the preferred Armor module because its shockwave damage amplification pushes Orbless much farther than neutral alternatives. Shockwave Frequency is the best ACP substat according to the guide, while the remaining Armor substats depend on whether the tower is wall-based or leaning toward glass cannon survival. Space Displacer is rejected because Inner Land Mines can cause deaths outside Spotlight, breaking the whole point of the build. Generator modules: Galaxy Compressor is the default best end-state Generator because it helps push GT and BH toward permanence while also improving Death Wave uptime. Package Chance, Enemy Health Level Skip, Coins per Kill, and Cash Bonus are the key Generator substats, with Enemy Attack Level Skip becoming more valuable once the build exits Orbless and needs to stretch survival. Singularity Harness is the alternative when GT and BH uptime is not yet high. It needs a synced Coin Bot to compete, and it usually falls behind Galaxy Compressor once cooldown compression is already strong enough. Core modules: Multiverse Nexus is the preferred Core module for most accounts because the guide claims it can reach permanent GT and BH for under roughly 12k stones, whereas natural permanent GT and BH would cost far more. The minimum desired Core substats are Death Wave Cooldown, Golden Tower Cooldown, and Spotlight Angle, with Golden Tower Bonus, Death Wave Quantity, and Spotlight Bonus listed as stretch goals. Dimension Core is presented only as a niche option for towers that already have natural permanent GT and BH, and Om Chip is explicitly rejected because boss-focused Spotlight rotation disrupts the natural beam sweep across Black Holes.

title: Orbless Guide Perk Plan
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orbless Guide Perk Plan mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic orbless one-liner, a live tracker state, or a single stat definition page.
content: Orbless Guide Perk Plan. The perk shell wants all 4 options, as many bans as possible, and mature perk labs. First perk choice is Perk Wave Requirement. Free Upgrade and Interest are the cleanest universal bans because Free Upgrades poison the devo shell and Interest does not matter to a late-game Orbless farm. Absolute Defense is a spare-slot ban if room exists, while trade-off bans depend on the survival branch being used. Perk Wave Requirement, Coin Trade-Off, Golden Tower Bonus, Black Hole Duration or bonus support, Death Wave Quantity, Coins, Spotlight Bonus, and Cash are the perks the guide wants as soon as possible. Damage, the tower-damage-versus-boss-health trade-off, and Chain Lightning Damage are intentionally delayed until the run needs them for kill maintenance instead of taking them immediately and ruining the early Orbless window. Defense, Health, Health Regen, Bounce Shot, Land Mine Damage, Random Ultimate Weapon, and other Ultimate Weapon perks are situational filler choices once the main economy priorities are already secured.

title: Orbless Guide Strategy Tips
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Orbless Guide Strategy Tips mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic orbless one-liner, a live tracker state, or a single stat definition page.
content: Orbless Guide Strategy Tips. Bullet Orbless progression: Target Priority 2 on In Spotlight is the operating rule, and because that targeting no longer protects against every chip source during downtime, bullet builds commonly need a Wall-style survival shell behind them. The raw upgrade order is cards first, then core Damage and crit stats if bullet Orbless is the only planned kill shell, then Damage / Meter, Attack Speed, Multishot Chance, Bounce Shot Chance, Rapid Fire Chance, Land Mine Chance, Land Mine Damage, and finally damage perks. If the tower plans to transition into another Orbless shell later, permanent battle upgrades should be delayed and reversible card swaps should do more of the balancing work. Chain Lightning transitions: Chain Lightning Orbless normally starts after bullet Orbless, not before it. Because CL procs from bullet hits, Target Priority 2 is still needed to minimize spillage, and the CL damage perk should wait until Spotlight kills are no longer keeping pace. The guide repeatedly warns against pushing CL damage and quantity too high because the shell becomes very hard to localize once chain damage gets too aggressive. Spotlight Missiles transitions: SLM Orbless effectively needs Smart Missiles so Missile Amp labs and meaningful explosion radius can do their work. Maxed Spotlight Missiles and Smart Missile Amp labs are expected, while Smart Missile Radius needs to be researched and then tuned to the tower rather than blindly maxed for every account. SLM is described as the most AFK Orbless branch because it naturally targets inside Spotlight, scales through repeated Missile Amp tagging, and can support glass-cannon juggling by making bullets harmless enough to juggle instead of kill. The SLM upgrade order is simpler than bullet Orbless: cards first, then damage and crit upgrades, then Land Mine Chance and Land Mine Damage, then the damage perk layer.

title: Perks Guide Overview
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Perks Guide Overview mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not the base perks rules page, a single perk definition, or a generic one-line pick order.
content: Perks Guide Overview. Perks are one of the earliest run-level accelerators in the game, so even modest perk support can let an account push beyond its normal short-run ceiling. The tradeoff is that weak perk labs make the system volatile enough to ruin a run instead of saving it. Relevant site data matches that framing: perks unlock through the Unlock Perks milestone at Tier 2 Wave 150, start appearing at wave 200 after the unlock lab is finished, are unavailable in tournaments, and begin with only 2 choices unless Perk Option Quantity is researched. The guide therefore treats perks less as a static tier list and more as a decision framework built around run goal, account maturity, and the opportunity cost of every pick that enters or leaves the run pool.

title: Perks Guide Early Priorities
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Perks Guide Early Priorities mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not the base perks rules page, a single perk definition, or a generic one-line pick order.
content: Perks Guide Early Priorities. Early perks are described as weak because the player starts with 2 choices, no banned perks, and no first perk choice. That means low-roll offerings can trap the run between two bad trade-off choices before the perk system is mature enough to be reliable. The guide treats one level of Perk Option Quantity as the real starting breakpoint because moving from 2 choices to 3 sharply reduces how often early runs are bricked by double-bad offerings. Ban Perks becomes the next efficient early support lab. The first bans should usually target trade-off perks or other low-value fillers that do nothing for the current playstyle, while lower-impact fillers such as Interest can wait until the later ban slots. Perks are still worth that detour because they affect the short term immediately through individual runs, daily missions, and weekly missions, while their long-term lab burden is modest compared with many other progression systems.

title: Perks Guide Established Towers
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Perks Guide Established Towers mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not the base perks rules page, a single perk definition, or a generic one-line pick order.
content: Perks Guide Established Towers. The established-tower section is aimed at the player entering midgame: usually 3 perk choices, possibly First Perk Choice, most lab slots unlocked, farming runs reaching about 1000 waves or more, and milestone pushes that are close but not trivial. The guide frames perk thinking through short-term versus long-term value. Short term means the current run and mission progress, while long term means the labs, relics, themes, and other account-level gains those runs are funding. That distinction is why the guide does not use one universal perk order. Coin runs, milestone pushes, and event-specific goals all want different timing even when they start from the same perk shell.

title: Perks Guide Coin Runs
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Perks Guide Coin Runs mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not the base perks rules page, a single perk definition, or a generic one-line pick order.
content: Perks Guide Coin Runs. Perk Wave Requirement is still the first priority for coin runs because earlier perk access snowballs through the entire run. Even with 4 options and First Perk Choice, the guide assumes the player may still miss one of the three copies, so it says to take the perk whenever it appears. If the account is farming under roughly 2000 waves, the immediate coin picks often win. That includes the coin trade-off perk and Golden Tower Bonus whenever they appear in a run that can survive them cleanly. Longer low-tier runs are different because the guide expects the real coin yield to arrive much later. In those runs, long-duration value from perks such as Free Upgrade Chance for All, Increase Max Game Speed by +1.00, and the Enemies Damage -50%, but Tower Damage -50% trade-off can outpace a greedier early coin grab. Once the run already has its perk-wave shell and long-run support online, the remaining picks fall back toward obvious economy tools first and generic survivability after that, with Defense Percent, Damage, and Health used as filler when better coin choices are absent.

title: Perks Guide Milestone Runs
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Perks Guide Milestone Runs mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not the base perks rules page, a single perk definition, or a generic one-line pick order.
content: Perks Guide Milestone Runs. Milestone runs shift the perk question from economy to survival. Perk Wave Requirement is still first in deep pushes because earlier perk access compounds into more survival picks later in the same run. For long milestone runs, the guide likes the Free Upgrade standard perk very early because expensive battle upgrades eventually outpace what one wave of income can buy manually. In that context, the perk is solving scaling, not just saving clicks. The raw guide also recommends micromanaging the opening waves with Cash support if needed so the tower can finish expensive battle rows such as Crit Factor, Bounce Shot Range, Land Mine Radius, and Damage / Meter before those rows become too expensive to finish cleanly. Super Crit, Enemy Attack Level Skip, and Enemy Health Level Skip get special mention because they are among the rows whose cash cost ramps fastest. When those mechanics are active in the run, early perk value is partly measured by how much sooner they can be pushed. Shorter milestone pushes compress the order: Defense Percent, Health, and attack perks can outrank Free Upgrade in shallow pushes, but the guide still warns not to underrate Free Upgrade once battle upgrades are no longer affordable by normal wave income.

title: Perks Guide Perk Reduction
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Perks Guide Perk Reduction mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not the base perks rules page, a single perk definition, or a generic one-line pick order.
content: Perks Guide Perk Reduction. The guide treats perk reduction as two different systems. The long-term route is lab driven through Ban Perks, Perk Option Quantity, First Perk Choice, Standard Perk Bonus, and the Waves Required lab. The short-term route is in-run management through Perk Wave Requirement and careful pool cleanup. The lab route is more reliable because it changes every future run. Perk Wave Requirement is still powerful, but it is a chance-based in-run fix rather than guaranteed structure. The overlooked short-term trick is to remove dead perks from the current pool even when they are not immediately useful. The guide example is taking an otherwise useless Ultimate Weapon perk so it cannot appear again later in the run. That logic works because a weapon-specific Ultimate Weapon perk can only appear once per weapon, so consuming a low-value option early can open later offerings for stronger perks. The warning is that perk timing becomes less forgiving after 20 total perks, because the base waves between offers rise by bracket. A bad cleanup pick can therefore cost more than one future perk if it delays access across a bracket shift.

title: Perks Guide Priority Routes
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Perks Guide Priority Routes mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not the base perks rules page, a single perk definition, or a generic one-line pick order.
content: Perks Guide Priority Routes. These route examples assume max perk quantity and unusually favorable offerings. The guide presents them as planning references for perk-wave timing and goal shaping, not as rigid universal scripts. Perk Wave Requirement is assumed to be the first pick unless the run has a special one-off objective, because passing it up always costs some amount of future perk access and therefore reduces later flexibility. Generic long-term route: (3) Perk Wave Requirement (4) Enemies Damage -50%, but Tower Damage -50% (5) Increase Max Game Speed by +1.00 (10) Free Upgrade Chance for All +5.0% (17) Coin perks such as x1.80 Coins, but Tower Max Health -70% and Golden Tower Bonus x1.5 (23) Defense Percent +4.00 (28) Damage (33) Max Health (41) Ultimate Weapon perks Reduced-perk route: (3) Perk Wave Requirement (4) Increase Max Game Speed by +1.00 (17) Single-quantity perks such as the -50/-50 trade-off, the x1.80 coin trade-off, and Ultimate Weapon perks (22) Bounce Shot or Orbs (##) Goal-specific favorites for the current run

title: Perks Guide Common Pitfalls
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Perks Guide Common Pitfalls mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not the base perks rules page, a single perk definition, or a generic one-line pick order.
content: Perks Guide Common Pitfalls. The guide calls the Waves Required lab a poor place to overinvest once the early levels are done. It still has value, but the raw warning is that the cost and time climb fast while the practical appeal falls off after roughly level 10. Auto Pick Perks is explicitly not treated as an early or mid-priority perk lab. The guide sees it as expensive, slow, and dependent on the rest of the perk shell already being strong enough that automated choices are not actively harmful. First Perk Choice is still considered a mandatory eventual unlock, but the guide warns against overreading it. First Perk Choice does not guarantee trade-off perks, so it cannot force x1.80 Coins, but Tower Max Health -70% onto the first offer.

title: SMAX Devo Guide Overview
disambiguation: This chunk is about the SMAX Devo Guide Overview mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo one-liner, a single stat definition, or a live build readout.
content: SMAX Devo Guide Overview. SMAX Devo is a damage-oriented devo branch built around hoarding and eHP tanking a stack until synchronized Black Hole and Golden Tower activations pull that stack together for a delayed Smart Missiles clear. The guide treats Smart Missiles as the first real payout shell, not the end state. Once missile volleys stop clearing cleanly, the build is expected to pivot into Orb Devo and finally into a blender finish instead of pretending the same shell still scales forever. Relevant site data matches that framing because SMAX depends on synced Ultimate Weapon timing, controlled devo workshop rows, Black Hole lab support for protectors, and survivability layers that keep enemies alive long enough to die inside the intended bonus window.

title: SMAX Devo Guide Requirements
disambiguation: This chunk is about the SMAX Devo Guide Requirements mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo one-liner, a single stat definition, or a live build readout.
content: SMAX Devo Guide Requirements. The hard opener is Black Hole and Golden Tower in sync, with Multiverse Nexus allowed as the same kind of temporary bridge the other devo guides use when natural sync is not ready yet. Smart Missiles also needs to stay in sync with that shared bonus window. Shockwave size is tuned rather than maxed. The guide calls out about 1.4 for non-Wall setups and about 1.65 to 1.75 when Wall is part of the build, because the goal is to juggle basics toward trim positions instead of scattering the full pile. The workshop must already be devoed heavily into defensive options, and the account still needs enough damage depth to cash-max the important offense rows early in the run. The raw benchmark given is workshop Damage at roughly 5000 or higher. This is not a cheap devo variant. The guide explicitly frames SMAX as stone, lab, and enhancement dependent because the damage shell has to be strong enough to burst stacked enemies without giving up devo control too early.

title: SMAX Devo Guide Workshop Devo
disambiguation: This chunk is about the SMAX Devo Guide Workshop Devo mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo one-liner, a single stat definition, or a live build readout.
content: SMAX Devo Guide Workshop Devo. Attack rows left at zero: Attack Speed Multishot Chance Rapid Fire Chance Bounce Shot Chance Defense rows left at zero or tightly controlled: Thorn Damage stays at zero in workshop and is only raised during the run until basics are trimmed cleanly, usually ending around 34% Knockback Chance Orbs Shockwave Size stays at its tuned shuffle value Land Mine Chance Land Mine Radius Utility rows left at zero until the blender exit: Free Attack Upgrade Free Defense Upgrade Free Utility Upgrade Optional rows kept low for variant paths: Critical Chance for players extending damage devo longer Range kept at the 30m base for alternate positioning plans Land Mine Damage only for Land Mine Stun support or Spotlight-driven land-mine offshoots

topic: SMAX Devo Guide Cards and Support
title: SMAX Devo Guide Cards and Support
disambiguation: This chunk is about the SMAX Devo Guide Cards and Support mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo one-liner, a single stat definition, or a live build readout.
content: SMAX Devo Guide Cards and Support. Required cards: Coins Critical Coin Cash Enemy Balance Health Extra Defense Berzerker Damage Critical Chance Economy cards: Wave Skip Wave Accelerator Defensive swaps: Health Regen when the tower is using Wall or Wormhole Redirector Recovery Package Chance when Wall is absent or the run is leaning on Galaxy Compressor package triggers Optional utility cards: Ultimate Crit Land Mine Stun only after land-mine damage is no longer ruining the stack and a strong Land Mine Radius setup exists The guide strongly prefers maxed Black Hole Coin Bonus and maxed Black Hole Damage so the stack produces more coins and protectors stop stalling the transition timing. Death Wave and Spotlight are treated as major accelerants rather than absolute requirements. Death Wave adds health, coins, and cells, while Spotlight adds another coin multiplier on the same stacked kill window. A 25-second Black Hole duration with perk support is the named protector breakpoint because at max Black Hole Damage the guide expects protectors to die in two Black Hole cycles before the Orb Devo transition. Extra Black Hole, Garlic Thorns, lower synced cooldowns on Black Hole, Golden Tower, Death Wave, and Smart Missiles, Ultimate Crit, and a synced Coin Bot when Galaxy Compressor is absent are all listed as meaningful upgrades once the base shell is already working. Relevant site data reinforces one of the guide implications: Smart Missiles has no dedicated unique Core module, so real SMAX support comes from sync control, shared Ultimate Weapon cooldown compression, and the normal Smart Missiles substats rather than from chasing a nonexistent missile-only unique module.

title: SMAX Devo Guide Run Plan
disambiguation: This chunk is about the SMAX Devo Guide Run Plan mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo one-liner, a single stat definition, or a live build readout.
content: SMAX Devo Guide Run Plan. The base loop is to hoard enemies, eHP tank the pile, then let synchronized Black Hole and Golden Tower pull the stack together so Smart Missiles can kill the bricks inside the payout window. Smart Missiles should be offset a few seconds after Black Hole instead of firing immediately. That delay gives Black Hole time to collect the stack into a tighter clump, and more Black Hole Damage can extend how long the missiles keep clearing that clump before the transition is needed. After setup is stable, run cash goes into offense first: Critical Chance, Critical Factor, Damage, Super Crit Chance, Super Crit Multiplier, and Enemy Health Level Skip. After the offense shell is healthy, cash shifts into defense: Enemy Attack Level Skip, Wall if the account has it, Health, Health Regen when a Wall or Wormhole Redirector plan exists, Defense Absolute, and Defense %. Thorn Damage is micromanaged rather than freely upgraded because basics are worth less than tanks, but the guide still wants them trimmed so they do not occupy the stack forever. Once Smart Missiles can no longer clear the stack in one volley, the run is supposed to proceed to Orb Devo. Once survival is failing outright, cash goes into the three Free Upgrade rows and the build exits into a blender finish until death.

title: SMAX Devo Guide Improvement Paths
disambiguation: This chunk is about the SMAX Devo Guide Improvement Paths mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo one-liner, a single stat definition, or a live build readout.
content: SMAX Devo Guide Improvement Paths. The guide treats survival improvements and damage improvements as the two real improvement buckets. Both matter because SMAX fails either when missiles stop killing cleanly or when the tower cannot survive long enough to wait for the payout window. For the Smart Missiles shell specifically, the guide rates Missile Amplifier, some Missile Radius, and more missile quantity as better real damage investments than simply dumping more stones into raw Smart Missiles damage. Cooldown reductions still have to respect sync. The named priority is lowering Black Hole, Golden Tower, and Smart Missiles together without breaking the timing relationship the whole build depends on.

disambiguation: This chunk is about the SMAX Devo Guide Perk Priorities mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo one-liner, a single stat definition, or a live build readout.
content: SMAX Devo Guide Perk Priorities. Economy perk priorities: Perk Wave Requirement Coin Trade-Off Golden Tower Bonus Black Hole Duration Coins Extra Death Wave Cash Damage Damage / Boss Health Trade-Off Defensive perk priorities: Regen Trade-Off, if the wall shell can actually survive it Health Regen Defense % Max Health Defense Absolute

title: SMAX Devo Guide Survival Priorities
disambiguation: This chunk is about the SMAX Devo Guide Survival Priorities mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo one-liner, a single stat definition, or a live build readout.
content: SMAX Devo Guide Survival Priorities. Low lifetime coin survival: In Tier 1 and Tier 2 starts, Defense Absolute is the first real crutch and is pushed to about 1000 workshop levels before Health takes over Health is then pushed toward roughly 5000 so it can be cash-maxed during the run Wormhole Redirector can make Health Regen matter later, but the guide warns that early Regen scaling is weak until the account is much deeper Lab survival goals: Defense % to level 23 so capped defense is reachable with an ancestral substat and maxed Standard Perk Bonus Death Wave Health Health lab to about level 50 Maxed Standard Perk Bonus Enemy Attack Level Skip support Early mid-game survival: Wormhole Redirector is treated as the default strongest survivability module once real module options exist The guide wants the highest-rarity Defense % substat available Mythic-or-better Land Mine Radius makes Land Mine Stun valuable late because it can lock enemies without ruining the stack Thorn Damage substats also help reach later Wall-thorns breakpoints and extend the closing blender phase

title: SMAX Devo Guide Thorns Trimming
disambiguation: This chunk is about the SMAX Devo Guide Thorns Trimming mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo one-liner, a single stat definition, or a live build readout.
content: SMAX Devo Guide Thorns Trimming. Thorn trimming is a separate control problem, not a mindless damage upgrade. Between each activation before Wall takes over, the goal is to reduce basics to as few as possible so tanks occupy more of the stack. Shockwave naturally shuffles tanks toward the back of the pile, so Thorn Damage and Shockwave Size are tuned together rather than treated as isolated rows. The raw starting point is about 15% to 20% Thorn Damage, then slowly raising it as basic spawn rates climb so basics are thinned without deleting too many tanks or breaking the stack apart.

title: SMAX Devo Guide Common Pitfalls
disambiguation: This chunk is about the SMAX Devo Guide Common Pitfalls mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic devo one-liner, a single stat definition, or a live build readout.
content: SMAX Devo Guide Common Pitfalls. The guide calls SMAX a damage-based build first, so underdeveloped stone, lab, or enhancement investment will make it stall earlier than cheaper devo shells. SMAX is less affected by Protectors than Orb Devo while the missile shell is still strong, but once missiles stop one-volleying the run can unravel quickly if the Black Hole support shell is not ready for the transition. Land Mine Stun is explicitly delayed until land-mine damage is irrelevant to the stack, because a premature land-mine setup kills the pile the build is trying to preserve.

title: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Overview
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Tier 1 Beginner Guide Overview mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic beginner summary, a single stat definition, or a live tracker build readout.
content: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Overview. Tier 1 Beginner Guide treats early progression as a turtle build where Defense Absolute and Thorns keep the tower alive long enough to unlock Tier 2. The raw guide is explicit that Tier 1 is the only tier where that shell remains reliable by itself. The guide is not telling players to perfect Tier 1 forever. The real path is to unlock Tier 2, keep farming Tier 1 until the early workshop rows can be maxed during runs, then pivot into a Health-based shell that can survive higher-tier scaling. Relevant site data supports that progression path because tier access is tied to milestone progression, Max Interest appears on the Tier 2 milestone table, and later survival systems such as Health, Defense %, Lifesteal, Knockback, Orb Speed, and Orbs already exist as tracker-backed mechanics that replace early Defense Absolute once the turtle shell stops scaling.

title: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Economy
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Economy mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic beginner summary, a single stat definition, or a live tracker build readout.
content: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Economy. Cash / Wave and Coins / Wave are the fastest early economy rows because flat per-wave payouts matter most before enemy density is high enough for kill-based income to dominate. Cash Bonus and Coins / Kill Bonus become more important once the account can pass roughly wave 100, because later waves spawn enough enemies for kill scaling to overtake the flat per-wave rows. Interest / Wave is still useful early, but the guide only wants light investment because Max Interest is capped at $50 until early milestone progression expands that rule. Current site milestone data shows Max Interest arriving much earlier than the older Discord phrasing suggests.

topic: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Turtle Shell
title: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Turtle Shell
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Turtle Shell mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic beginner summary, a single stat definition, or a live tracker build readout.
content: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Turtle Shell. Defense Absolute is the core early survival row, but the guide only asks for about 50 between-round workshop levels before shifting coin spending elsewhere. Small early Health upgrades are still encouraged so the tower has some buffer while the shell comes online. Defense % becomes the next between-round defensive priority after Defense Absolute is established, because the guide wants a simple turtle shell rather than an all-in single-stat stack. Thorns is the main damage source in the first stage. The guide specifically recommends buying clean thorn fractions such as 6%, 11%, 21%, and 26% so rounding does not quietly add an extra enemy hit.

topic: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Run Loop
title: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Run Loop
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Run Loop mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic beginner summary, a single stat definition, or a live tracker build readout.
content: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Run Loop. The in-run loop is intentionally simple: push Cash / Wave for roughly the first 5 to 9 waves, then Coins / Wave for roughly waves 10 to 20, then move into Cash Bonus and Coins / Kill Bonus until enemies start leaking through Defense Absolute. Once the turtle shell begins taking damage, the guide says to improve Defense Absolute in-run and only buy Thorns if the upgrade reaches the next meaningful breakpoint more efficiently than another Defense Absolute purchase. Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Run Loop is meant to be repeated, not optimized into a complex branching build. The goal is to turn early economy into a stable turtle shell, unlock Tier 2, and keep refining the same loop until step two rows can be maxed in normal runs.

topic: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot
title: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic beginner summary, a single stat definition, or a live tracker build readout.
content: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot. Economy after the turtle shell: Coins / Kill Bonus becomes the main long-run coin row because most later income comes from kills instead of flat per-wave payouts. Cash Bonus becomes the main in-run cash engine once enemy count is high enough to justify multiplicative cash scaling. Coins / Wave becomes low priority later and can simply be maxed once spending 20 million coins on it is no longer meaningful, while Cash / Wave remains an early-wave helper rather than a permanent centerpiece. Health-based survival package: Defense Absolute should stop being the main plan at this stage because the guide says higher progression is easier through Health than through a direct damage pivot. Health and Defense % become the real survival pair, while Lifesteal becomes the main healing source and only works from tower projectile damage. Knockback, Orb Speed, and Orbs become the crowd-control package that keeps normal enemies away from the tower long enough for Health and Lifesteal to matter, even though bosses will still make contact. Damage support for Lifesteal and crowd control: Attack Speed is the first support row because more projectile hits improve both Knockback uptime and Lifesteal frequency. Damage, Critical Chance, Critical Factor, and Damage / Meter all improve Lifesteal indirectly because they raise projectile damage per hit. Multishot, Rapid Fire Chance, and Bounce Shot Chance are added in that order as each earlier layer becomes maxable in-run, while Super Crit is strong later but can wait until spending 100 million coins is comfortable. Range can stay low for now because the guide says it does not help much yet.

title: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Tier 2 Transition
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Tier 1 Beginner Guide Tier 2 Transition mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic beginner summary, a single stat definition, or a live tracker build readout.
content: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Tier 2 Transition. Tier 1 Beginner Guide Tier 2 Transition says Tier 2 should be unlocked early but not farmed immediately. The raw guide describes Tier 2 as approximately x20 harder even though its coin payout is close to 2x Tier 1, so the account should keep farming Tier 1 first while the new Health shell is being built. The guide recommends checking Tier 2 every several runs after Tier 1 can reach about wave 1000. Around wave 300 in Tier 2, the higher Tier Coin Bonus should start beating Tier 1 for coins even if the run length is much shorter. Once Tier 2 becomes practical, Defense Absolute should stop receiving in-run priority. Health, Defense %, Knockback, Orb Speed, Orbs, and Lifesteal become the stable survival package there, while milestone progression around that transition keeps unlocking long-term account systems such as Perks.

title: Tier Rushing Guide Overview
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Tier Rushing Guide Overview mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic milestone summary, a one-card explainer, or a live run state readout.
content: Tier Rushing Guide Overview. Tier Rushing is a short-range progression tactic where the player swaps out their normal farming or milestone build for a one-time boss-survival shell meant only to reach the next early tier-unlock wave. The practical target is usually about wave 100, not a full stable run. The guide is explicit that Tier Rushing is more useful on earlier tiers where scaling is still weak. It is a method for forcing a small number of extra boss clears, not a replacement for a normal long-run build once the account can already farm or push that tier honestly. Relevant site data matches that framing because tier progression is milestone-gated, boss layers such as Death Defy and Energy Shield are real tracker-backed mechanics, and Tier 14 battle conditions directly weaken the classic Plasma Cannon plus Thorns finish that the guide relies on.

title: Tier Rushing Guide Survival Layers
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Tier Rushing Guide Survival Layers mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic milestone summary, a one-card explainer, or a live run state readout.
content: Tier Rushing Guide Survival Layers. Passive and semi-passive survival layers: Death Defy is the first survivability layer because it can ignore a lethal hit before most other death-prevention systems are spent, making every later layer stronger whenever it procs. Energy Shield buys one protected boss contact by default and can buy more if Energy Shield Extra Hits is unlocked, but its recharge is usually too long for Tier Rushing to expect many natural reuses during a short run. Plasma Cannon is paired with Thorns because a high enough Plasma Cannon hit can leave the boss low enough for the normal 99% Thorns breakpoint to finish it in one contact, reducing pressure on Death Defy and Energy Shield. Second Wind is the cleanest once-per-rush safety layer because it guarantees a survival window instead of depending on percentage rolls, and the raw guide notes that Second Wind Blast can help clear extra enemies during that invulnerable span. Manual boss-kill tools: Demon Mode is treated as a manual Second Wind with a longer duration, but it cannot be activated during Intro Sprint so the guide saves it for later in the sequence. Nuke is another manual boss answer and is more forgiving than Missile Barrage when used late, but it is inconsistent when underleveled and is intentionally saved as the last manual method. Missile Barrage is the earliest manual boss tool in the guide because it can preserve an Energy Shield charge on early boss waves, especially when Missile Amplifier research makes the barrage more reliable.

title: Tier Rushing Guide Timing Control
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Tier Rushing Guide Timing Control mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic milestone summary, a one-card explainer, or a live run state readout.
content: Tier Rushing Guide Timing Control. Speed and retry compression: Intro Sprint is valuable because Tier Rushing is retry-heavy. Faster early waves mean more attempts in the same time window and can also let a high-level Second Wind cover a second boss wave before the run slows down. Wave Accelerator is a niche extension tool rather than a mandatory card. The guide only values it when the reduced gap between waves helps Second Wind or Demon Mode reach another boss before their protective window expires. Boss arrival manipulation: Slow Aura is used as a timing lever, not just as a passive slow. The guide suggests equipping it to delay a boss so Second Wind or Demon Mode triggers later, then removing it before the next boss so the following hit arrives inside the remaining duration. Chrono Field can do the same job at a larger scale by being active for one boss but disabled for the next, letting the player choose which boss hit is delayed and which one arrives faster.

title: Tier Rushing Guide Run Sequence
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Tier Rushing Guide Run Sequence mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic milestone summary, a one-card explainer, or a live run state readout.
content: Tier Rushing Guide Run Sequence. The guide sequence starts by tanking the first boss with normal eHP if possible. If that fails, Missile Barrage is the first manual boss answer because it can save one of the later survival layers for the next boss wave instead of spending it immediately. Energy Shield is then expected to carry the next boss and may cover more than one if extra charges are unlocked. Once shield charges are gone, Second Wind becomes the next guaranteed extension layer and can often cover one or two more bosses depending on timing. After Second Wind is consumed, the guide says to deactivate Intro Sprint. Demon Mode is then activated just as the next boss hits so its invulnerability window has a chance to stretch into another boss wave instead of being wasted between waves. Nuke is held to the very end as the last manual boss kill. The run length after that point is heavily dependent on Death Defy rolls and boss spawn timing, so the guide expects repeated attempts until the player reaches the target unlock wave.

topic: Tier Rushing Guide Breakpoints and Limits
title: Tier Rushing Guide Breakpoints and Limits
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Tier Rushing Guide Breakpoints and Limits mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a generic milestone summary, a one-card explainer, or a live run state readout.
content: Tier Rushing Guide Breakpoints and Limits. The guide calls Tier Rushing effective only for very early milestone progress, usually up to around wave 100. Past that point the strategy loses value because the run shell is built from one-time tools rather than repeatable economy or survivability engines. Tier Rushing is stronger on earlier tiers where scaling is still soft, because the whole plan assumes bosses can be solved by stacking one-time layers such as Energy Shield, Plasma Cannon plus Thorns, Second Wind, Demon Mode, and Nuke in a deliberate order. Tier 14 is the explicit breakpoint where the guide says the strategy stops being reliable. The relevant site data explains why: Tier 14 battle conditions add Thorns Resistance and Plasma Cannon Resistance, directly weakening the standard Plasma Cannon plus Thorns boss finish the rush shell depends on. That limitation is why the guide treats Tier Rushing as a progression bridge rather than a permanent build. The goal is to unlock the next tier or collect an early milestone, then return to a real build instead of trying to push the same one-time shell indefinitely.

content: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Overview. Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide treats UW selection as a permanent progression decision because each purchase costs Power Stones, the next selection gets more expensive, and a weak early pick can delay every later sync or farming plan built on the roster. The raw ranking is Golden Tower first, then Black Hole, Death Wave, Spotlight, Chrono Field, Chain Lightning, Smart Missiles, Inner Land Mines, and Poison Swamp. The guide is directional rather than absolute, but it is explicit that early economy and reliable overlap value matter more than isolated late-game ceiling. Relevant site data supports that framing because Ultimate Weapons are bought from a rotating 3-choice offer, several of the strongest picks need labs or modules before their full value shows up, and sync tools such as Multiverse Nexus change timing without removing the long-term cost of permanent unlock order.

content: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Economy Core. Golden Tower is the default first pick because it is immediate income instead of delayed support. The raw guide calls it an instant 20% boost to both cash and coins, and current site data backs that economy-first role with Golden Tower Bonus and Golden Tower Duration labs unlocking at Tier 4 Wave 200. Black Hole stays second even though it feels weak on unlock because most of its value is lab-gated. Site data shows Black Hole Damage and Black Hole Coin Bonus unlocking at Tier 5 Wave 150 and Extra Black Hole at Tier 5 Wave 500, which matches the guide claim that BH becomes strong once coin stacking, protector damage, and overlap support are online. Death Wave now belongs in the early economy shell rather than the old late-support slot. The raw guide emphasizes that its coin, health, and cell rewards apply on hit instead of only on kill, and current site data confirms Death Wave Health, Death Wave Coins Bonus, and Death Wave Cell Bonus as real scaling rows that keep paying off even when the wave is no longer killing everything cleanly. That is why the guide keeps grouping Golden Tower, Black Hole, and Death Wave together. Their coin effects stack through shared timing, and Multiverse Nexus is useful as a temporary bridge because current site data shows it synchronizing those three UWs around an averaged cooldown while natural long-term sync is still being built.

Current site data shows Missile Amplifier, Missile Explosions, and Missile Radius as the important lab shell, which matches the raw guide claim that Smart Missiles eventually becomes the dominant late-game damage source but needs more investment before it cleanly surpasses cheaper midgame options.

topic: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Control and Midgame Damage
title: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Control and Midgame Damage
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Control and Midgame Damage mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a stone-cost table, a single Ultimate Weapon stat sheet, or a live account recommendation.
content: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Control and Midgame Damage. Chrono Field is the crowd-control pivot because it can become effectively permanent once the account can afford the duration investment. Site data confirms Chrono Field Duration at Tier 7 Wave 90 and explicitly notes that Chrono Field can sustain permanent uptime, which is why the raw guide values it so highly for survival and enemy pacing. The raw guide makes the 5th-pick timing conditional on lab speed support: if the account cannot keep a 3x lab boost running, Chrono Field should usually be taken as the 5th UW; if that lab acceleration exists continuously, it can slide later because the duration grind is less punishing. That timing rule is the main reason the ranking is not meant to be read as one rigid script for every account. Chain Lightning follows because it is a relatively cheap midgame damage bridge while Chrono Field is still being built. Site data shows Chain Lightning Shock unlocking at Tier 7 Wave 60 and then opening Shock Chance and Shock Multiplier, while Dimension Core further expands Shock stacking and doubles Shock chance and multiplier, which matches the guide claim that CL is strong for elites before full late-game missile scaling is ready.

topic: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Late-Game Specialists
title: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Late-Game Specialists
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Late-Game Specialists mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a stone-cost table, a single Ultimate Weapon stat sheet, or a live account recommendation.
content: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Late-Game Specialists. Smart Missiles becomes the main late-game killer once the account can fund its lab shell and pair it with Spotlight. The guide ranks it behind Chain Lightning only because Missile Amplifier and Missile Radius take time to mature, not because the end-state damage ceiling is lower. Inner Land Mines is a specialist control pick rather than a bad weapon. The raw guide values its stun window on bosses and elites, notes that it is comparatively cheap to upgrade into visible impact, and current site data supports that role through Inner Mine Stun plus module hooks such as Magnetic Hook and Space Displacer that extend how often Inner Land Mines actually connect. The guide also makes Inner Land Mines contextual rather than universally late-best. It says the weapon was stronger in an older pure-damage meta than in the current hybrid environment, so the ranking is about account timing and support value rather than about the weapon being weak by itself. Poison Swamp remains last because the guide only wants it after Chrono Field is already developed and preferably after CF+ support exists. Current site data shows Swamp Radius and Poison Swamp Stun as the early lab shell, while Chrono Loop is the named CF+ row that reinforces the same long-control requirement; the raw guide is clear that Poison Swamp underperforms when enemies are not being controlled long enough for the ramping damage profile to matter.
