title: Event Guide Overview
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Event Guide Overview mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a mission reward table, a live event state readout, or a generic summary outside the event guide.
content: Event Guide Overview. The event guide is a strategy reference for finishing event quests efficiently so medals and relic thresholds are missed less often. It assumes some quests naturally favor later-game accounts because they may depend on specific unlocks, Ultimate Weapons, cards, or other progression gates. The guide treats event success as maximizing medals earned per event rather than tunnel-visioning one awkward quest at the expense of the full event shop and relic cycle.

title: Event Guide Event Context
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Event Guide Event Context mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a mission reward table, a live event state readout, or a generic summary outside the event guide.
content: Event Guide Event Context. Events are a medal-and-relic cycle with a store that also sells themes, relics, bots, and related long-term account upgrades. Each event contains multiple quests that award medals when their tiers are completed, while relics are awarded at medal thresholds during the current event. Because relics and shop value depend on how many medals are earned during each event, the guide pushes broad quest coverage rather than only the easiest mission types.

title: Event Guide General Methods
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Event Guide General Methods mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a mission reward table, a live event state readout, or a generic summary outside the event guide.
content: Event Guide General Methods. Many event quests progress naturally just by letting the game run, starting labs, buying cards, and continuing ordinary farming or pushing runs. WAWSIS, meaning Wave Accelerator, Wave Skip, and Intro Sprint, is repeatedly recommended as the speed tool for reaching useful waves quickly or forcing stronger enemy waves sooner. If an event quest requires a specific Ultimate Weapon that is not owned, the guide calls out the Random Ultimate Weapon Perk as the fallback route for making the quest completable.

title: Event Guide Core Quests
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Event Guide Core Quests mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a mission reward table, a live event state readout, or a generic summary outside the event guide.
content: Event Guide Core Quests. Kill [x] enemy: Most kill quests are straightforward, but elite targets become more efficient in higher tiers where elites spawn earlier. Enemy Balance is highlighted because it raises enemies per wave and can produce double elites with mastery, while Wave Accelerator reduces dead time between spawns. Reach wave [x] on any tier: Use a low tier where long survival is easy and stack the quest with other passive objectives. WAWSIS is the recommended speed method when the goal is finishing the quest quickly rather than multitasking it. Reach wave [x] without any cards equipped: The guide treats this as a slow but simple wave-60 objective on highest tier minus two. It does not need special interactions beyond enduring the run without card support.

title: Event Guide Survival Quests
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Event Guide Survival Quests mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a mission reward table, a live event state readout, or a generic summary outside the event guide.
content: Event Guide Survival Quests. Take no damage for [x] consecutive waves: Drop to Tier 1 and lean on strong Defense Absolute. Extra Defense and Fortress can help if needed, while Wave Accelerator speeds the timer and Wave Skip or Intro Sprint do not help because skipped waves do not count for the quest. Kill [x] bosses outside of tower range: Go to a low tier where bosses die to bounce shots outside range. Death Wave trivializes the quest when owned because Death Wave kills count as outside tower range, and WAWSIS is the main speed-up tool. Death defy [x] times / let energy shield save: Pick the highest tier that can be entered, equip Intro Sprint, and let bosses hit the tower. Energy Shield and Death Defy are the key mechanics, while Second Wind can absorb a failure point when neither one procs.

title: Event Guide Active Quests
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Event Guide Active Quests mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a mission reward table, a live event state readout, or a generic summary outside the event guide.
content: Event Guide Active Quests. Kill enemies while in Demon Mode / kill enemies with Nuke: Use the highest tier that can be entered with Wave Accelerator and Enemy Balance equipped. Remove one-shot or direct-damage support such as Death Ray, Extra Orb, and damage cards, disable damage Ultimate Weapons like Spotlight, Smart Missiles, and Chain Lightning, then wait for the sprint to end or the cap to fill before activating Demon Mode and Nuke together. Stun enemies using Land Mine Stun card / kill enemies using workshop landmines: Drop to a low tier and wait. Enemy Balance is excellent because it produces more bodies for land mines to hit, and disabling damage Ultimate Weapons can help preserve targets, except Spotlight which should remain on because it increases landmine damage. Skip [x] waves: Although the intended tool is the Wave Skip card, the guide says Intro Sprint completes the quest more quickly and WAWSIS is the maximum-speed version. Buy cards / buy modules / merge to get modules: These quests are lower priority because they cost gems. Card buying can auto-complete if all cards are already maxed, while merge-to-get-modules can also progress from rare boss drops when module drop-rate labs are developed.

title: Event Guide Ultimate Weapon Quests
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Event Guide Ultimate Weapon Quests mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a mission reward table, a live event state readout, or a generic summary outside the event guide.
content: Event Guide Ultimate Weapon Quests. Hit the same enemy with [x] smart missiles: Go to the highest tier possible with Energy Shield or Second Wind and trigger Missile Barrage as the boss is about to hit. Without Missile Barrage, the guide treats the quest as RNG-dependent because the boss must stay alive while missiles keep landing. WAWSIS helps reach tougher bosses faster. Kill [x] enemies inside of Spotlight: This is treated as one of the easiest Ultimate Weapon quests because simply farming with Spotlight active will finish it over time, and WAWSIS only speeds completion. Kill [x] enemies with Inner Land Mines / hit with Inner Land Mines: Higher tiers make the quest easier because enemies push far enough inward to touch the mines. The guide also calls out Magnetic Hook and Space Displacer as helpers that move Inner Land Mines farther out or supply ILM coverage even when the weapon is not owned, although the damage can be reduced. Have [x] enemies in the same Black Hole: The guide expects this to happen naturally. Devo builds do it especially well, while Black Hole duration support, higher-wave spawn rates, Enemy Balance, and Protectors all make it easier to hold large groups together. Poison [x] enemies with Poison Swamp: This is harder than it looks because Poison Swamp is often fully inside tower range. The guide offers two routes: use the Poison Swamp radius perk plus a strong base radius, or minimize range support so the swamp reaches outside tower range. Enemy Balance speeds both methods by adding more bodies into the swamp. Kill [x] enemies with Smart Missiles: Lower-tier runs complete the quest steadily. If Missile Barrage is unlocked, it can be paired with the Demon Mode and Nuke strategy, and Enemy Balance again raises target volume. Hit [x] enemies with Chain Lightning: This is straightforward once Chain Lightning is unlocked, especially with high attack speed. Wave Accelerator and Enemy Balance are the main speed tools because they create more rapid hit opportunities.

title: Coin Guide Overview
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Coin Guide Overview mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a calculator output, tracker-specific UI behavior, or an unrelated game-system summary outside the coin guide.
content: Coin Guide Overview. Coins are an important part of progress, and building coin economy correctly early helps the account progress more smoothly later. As more tools that accelerate coin earning are unlocked, the same multiplier and syncing ideas continue to scale the economy instead of becoming obsolete. The coin guide is about how coins are earned and what needs to be considered to keep pushing coin income higher over time. Most long-term economy comes from Coins / Kill rather than Coins / Wave. The guide therefore recommends focusing on synchronized Ultimate Weapon activations and combining as many multipliers as possible on the same kill windows.

title: Coin Guide Coins / Wave
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Coin Guide Coins / Wave mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a calculator output, tracker-specific UI behavior, or an unrelated game-system summary outside the coin guide.
content: Coin Guide Coins / Wave. Coins / Wave is the weakest source of coins because fewer multipliers scale it compared with kill-based income. Coins / Wave still has early-game value, especially in the earliest part of Tier 1 and again while first unlocking higher tiers. Because its scaling ceiling is limited, the guide recommends stopping Coins / Wave lab investment by about level 20, and many accounts can stop earlier without losing much long-term value.

title: Coin Guide Coins / Kill
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Coin Guide Coins / Kill mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a calculator output, tracker-specific UI behavior, or an unrelated game-system summary outside the coin guide.
content: Coin Guide Coins / Kill. Coins / Kill is where the vast majority of coins will come from once the account is past the very earliest stages. Understanding kill-based coin income means understanding both how multipliers stack and how timed coin systems are synchronized.

title: Coin Guide Multipliers
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Coin Guide Multipliers mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a calculator output, tracker-specific UI behavior, or an unrelated game-system summary outside the coin guide.
content: Coin Guide Multipliers. All coin multipliers multiply with each other when they affect the same enemy at the same time. That means packs, themes, Coins / Kill workshop, Ultimate Weapon coin bonuses, and similar effects become strongest when their overlap is maximized instead of drifting apart. Because of multiplicative stacking, adding a new multiplier is often more effective than heavily upgrading a multiplier that is already far above baseline. Example: Black Hole can reach x11 and Golden Tower can reach x20.75. When both are active on the same kill window, enemies drop x228.25 the normal coins.

title: Coin Guide Syncing
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Coin Guide Syncing mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a calculator output, tracker-specific UI behavior, or an unrelated game-system summary outside the coin guide.
content: Coin Guide Syncing. Ultimate Weapons and Bots are not active for the entire run, so syncing means making them activate together as often as possible to stack their coin value. The core syncing rule is simple: cooldowns should be exact multiples of each other, with 1:1 being the most common long-term target. Example: Golden Tower starts at 300 seconds and Black Hole starts at 200 seconds. A 1:1 sync happens when Golden Tower is reduced to 200 seconds so it always activates with Black Hole. A 2:1 sync alternative is reducing Black Hole to 150 seconds so Black Hole activates twice for each Golden Tower activation. The guide includes a Golden Tower and Death Wave to Black Hole sync chart where only exact equal activation starting points count as synced. In that chart, high values shown in yellow mean frequent syncs, while dark blue means rare or no syncs. Multiverse Nexus can mimic sync by synchronizing Death Wave, Golden Tower, and Black Hole through averaged cooldown timing with a penalty. A 2:1 sync or higher is harder to maintain because more upgrades must be saved and purchased together to avoid breaking the ratio. At 1:1, Golden Tower and Black Hole only need one cooldown upgrade each before either is changed again, but at 2:1 Golden Tower needs two matching upgrades for every one Black Hole cooldown step. If the needed stones are not saved before changing one side of the pair, the sync breaks and shared activations happen less often.

title: Coin Guide Coins / Kill Sources
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Coin Guide Coins / Kill Sources mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a calculator output, tracker-specific UI behavior, or an unrelated game-system summary outside the coin guide.
content: Coin Guide Coins / Kill Sources. This guide lists the major unlocks that increase Coins / Kill, either by raising coin bonus directly or by increasing the underlying Coins / Kill stat. Packs: Paid coin multipliers from the starter pack, epic pack, and disable ads. Also increases Coins / Wave. Coin Card: Card-based coin multiplier that increases as the card level increases. Also increases Coins / Wave. Enemy Balance: Indirectly increases coins by spawning more enemies that can drop coins. Tier: Tier progression increases coin value as the tier ladder rises. Also increases Coins / Wave. Themes: Medal-unlocked theme ownership increases coin income. Also increases Coins / Wave. Relics: Specific relic bonuses increase coins as part of permanent account progression. Also increases Coins / Wave. Coins / Kill: Direct workshop and lab investment into the Coins / Kill stat itself. Golden Tower: Ultimate Weapon coin source with its own supporting lab path. Black Hole: Ultimate Weapon source that requires its lab for the coin bonus portion. Spotlight: Ultimate Weapon source that requires its lab for the coin bonus portion. Death Wave: Ultimate Weapon source that requires its lab for the coin bonus portion. Coin Bot: Event-shop bot that needs medal upgrades to scale its value.

title: Coin Guide Daily Missions
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Coin Guide Daily Missions mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not a calculator output, tracker-specific UI behavior, or an unrelated game-system summary outside the coin guide.
content: Coin Guide Daily Missions. Daily Missions are a final source of coins outside the main kill-based economy loop. Early game, daily rewards can be a large part of total coin income, so unlocking as many tiers as possible is a valid way to raise those rewards sooner. Because Daily Mission coin rewards are ultimately limited to the tens of millions, they become a very small part of total income once the core coin economy is mature.

topic: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Economy with Cash Bonus, Cash / Wave, Coins / Kill Bonus, Coins / Wave, Interest / Wave, Max Interest, and Milestone Tier Progression
title: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Economy with Cash Bonus, Cash / Wave, Coins / Kill Bonus, Coins / Wave, Interest / Wave, Max Interest, and Milestone Tier Progression
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between the Tier 1 beginner economy loop and the workshop or milestone systems behind it, not the individual mechanics. It is not a universal endgame economy plan or a pure formula page.
content: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Economy with Cash Bonus, Cash / Wave, Coins / Kill Bonus, Coins / Wave, Interest / Wave, Max Interest, and Milestone Tier Progression. Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Economy starts on Cash / Wave and Coins / Wave because those flat rows pay out immediately in short early runs when enemy kills are still sparse. Cash Bonus and Coins / Kill Bonus take over later because the guide expects enemy density to rise after roughly wave 100, which is the point where kill-based scaling starts beating the flat per-wave rows. Interest / Wave is still part of the plan, but only in moderation. Max Interest is the limiting rule early on, and Milestone Tier Progression is what eventually relaxes that cap so the guide can stop treating interest as a small early-game bonus.
interaction_summary: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Economy begins with flat per-wave income because early runs lack kill density, then shifts toward Cash Bonus and Coins / Kill Bonus as waves lengthen. Interest / Wave is useful only lightly at first because Max Interest stays capped until later milestone progression expands that ceiling.

topic: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Overview, Step 1 Turtle Shell, and Step 1 Run Loop with Defense Absolute, Health, Defense %, and Thorns
title: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Overview, Step 1 Turtle Shell, and Step 1 Run Loop with Defense Absolute, Health, Defense %, and Thorns
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between the Tier 1 beginner turtle shell and its core defensive rows, not the individual mechanics. It is not a general EHP guide or a final-tier tanking recommendation.
content: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Overview, Step 1 Turtle Shell, and Step 1 Run Loop with Defense Absolute, Health, Defense %, and Thorns. Tier 1 Beginner Guide Overview says Tier 1 is the only tier where a true turtle shell is reliable, and Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Turtle Shell explains why: Defense Absolute is allowed to erase most incoming normal-wave chip damage while the build is still weak. Health and Defense % matter even in that shell because the guide does not want Defense Absolute treated as a fully isolated stat. Small Health growth and later Defense % levels keep the tower from collapsing the moment enemy damage rises above the flat Defense Absolute threshold. Thorns is the actual damage engine inside the shell, which is why Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Run Loop keeps telling the player to buy clean thorn breakpoints in-run when those upgrades reduce enemy contact more efficiently than another Defense Absolute purchase.
mechanics: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Turtle Shell
Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Run Loop
interaction_summary: The early Tier 1 shell works because Defense Absolute removes most normal chip damage, Health supplies a small buffer, Defense % strengthens that buffer, and Thorns converts enemy contact into the actual kill method. Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 1 Run Loop keeps reinvesting into whichever part of that shell is currently failing.

topic: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot with Health, Defense %, Lifesteal, Attack Speed, Damage, Critical Chance, Critical Factor, and Damage / Meter
title: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot with Health, Defense %, Lifesteal, Attack Speed, Damage, Critical Chance, Critical Factor, and Damage / Meter
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between the Tier 1 beginner health pivot and the projectile-damage systems that support it, not the individual mechanics. It is not a late-game damage guide or a standalone lifesteal formula page.
content: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot with Health, Defense %, Lifesteal, Attack Speed, Damage, Critical Chance, Critical Factor, and Damage / Meter. Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot is explicit that Defense Absolute should stop being the main plan once real progression starts, because Health and Defense % scale more naturally into higher tiers. Lifesteal becomes the central recovery mechanic in that same pivot, but only because Health gives the tower something worth refilling and because Lifesteal works from projectile damage instead of from thorn contact. Attack Speed improves how often Lifesteal can trigger, while Damage, Critical Chance, Critical Factor, and Damage / Meter all make each heal larger by increasing projectile damage per hit. The guide therefore treats those attack rows as support for survivability first, not as a pure damage-race package.
mechanics: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot
interaction_summary: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot replaces flat turtle defense with a Health and Defense % shell that is sustained by Lifesteal. Attack Speed raises heal frequency, while Damage, Critical Chance, Critical Factor, and Damage / Meter all raise the projectile damage that Lifesteal scales from.

topic: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot and Tier 2 Transition with Knockback Chance, Knockback Force, Orb Speed, Orbs, Health, and Lifesteal
title: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot and Tier 2 Transition with Knockback Chance, Knockback Force, Orb Speed, Orbs, Health, and Lifesteal
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between the Tier 1 beginner crowd-control package and the survival shell it supports, not the individual mechanics. It is not a general orb farming guide or a boss-control claim.
content: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot and Tier 2 Transition with Knockback Chance, Knockback Force, Orb Speed, Orbs, Health, and Lifesteal. Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot ties Knockback Chance and Knockback Force directly to Orbs. The point is not generic crowd control by itself; it is to keep enemies in orbital kill range so fewer bodies ever make contact with the tower. Orb Speed matters to that same plan because faster orbits make those Orbs connect more reliably, which turns knockback from a stall tool into a real kill-delivery system for normal enemies. Tier 1 Beginner Guide Tier 2 Transition keeps that package intact because Health and Lifesteal are still needed for boss hits, but the guide wants Knockback Chance, Knockback Force, Orb Speed, and Orbs doing most of the normal-wave cleanup before those resources are spent.
mechanics: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot
interaction_summary: The post-turtle survival shell still gets hit by bosses, so Tier 1 Beginner Guide Step 2 Health Pivot uses Knockback Chance, Knockback Force, Orb Speed, and Orbs to thin normal enemies before they ever reach the tower. That keeps Health and Lifesteal focused on boss or leak recovery instead of constant chip cleanup.

topic: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Overview and Tier 2 Transition with Tier Unlock Requirement, Tier Coin Bonus, Milestone Tier Progression, Defense Absolute, Health, and Defense %
title: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Overview and Tier 2 Transition with Tier Unlock Requirement, Tier Coin Bonus, Milestone Tier Progression, Defense Absolute, Health, and Defense %
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between the Tier 1 beginner transition rules and the tier systems behind them, not the individual mechanics. It is not a universal tier-pushing guide or a pure milestone table summary.
content: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Overview and Tier 2 Transition with Tier Unlock Requirement, Tier Coin Bonus, Milestone Tier Progression, Defense Absolute, Health, and Defense %. Tier 1 Beginner Guide Overview treats the first Tier Unlock Requirement as a progression checkpoint rather than a signal to abandon Tier 1 immediately. Unlocking Tier 2 matters because it opens the next milestone table, but the guide still expects more farming on Tier 1 first. Tier 1 Beginner Guide Tier 2 Transition makes the tradeoff explicit: Tier Coin Bonus is better in Tier 2, yet the raw guide still calls Tier 2 much harder, so the account waits until shorter Tier 2 runs can actually beat long Tier 1 farms for coins. Milestone Tier Progression is why that move is still worth testing early. The first successful Tier 2 pushes begin unlocking future account power, but once the move is real the guide stops leaning on Defense Absolute and instead expects Health and Defense % to carry the new tier.
interaction_summary: Tier 1 Beginner Guide Overview treats Tier 2 access as an early milestone goal, but Tier 1 Beginner Guide Tier 2 Transition warns that the account should not fully move over until the Health shell is ready. Tier Unlock Requirement and Milestone Tier Progression open the tier, Tier Coin Bonus makes it eventually more profitable, and the guide drops Defense Absolute in favor of Health and Defense % once that move happens.

topic: Tier Rushing Guide Survival Layers and Run Sequence with Death Defy, Energy Shield, Plasma Cannon, Second Wind, and eHP Guide Round Triage
title: Tier Rushing Guide Survival Layers and Run Sequence with Death Defy, Energy Shield, Plasma Cannon, Second Wind, and eHP Guide Round Triage
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Tier Rushing boss survival order and the core defensive tools it stacks, not the individual mechanics. It is not a generic eHP guide or a boss damage formula page.
content: Tier Rushing Guide Survival Layers and Run Sequence with Death Defy, Energy Shield, Plasma Cannon, Second Wind, and eHP Guide Round Triage. Tier Rushing Guide Survival Layers is built around ordering, not just owning strong cards. Death Defy rolls before most other death prevention, so the guide treats it as the first passive extension layer rather than as a final emergency button. Energy Shield and Plasma Cannon then act as one boss package. Plasma Cannon pushes the boss low enough that Thorns can finish it cleanly, while Energy Shield buys the protected contact needed to cash in that boss kill without immediately consuming the rest of the rush shell. Energy Shield Extra Hits is the specific milestone support that can extend that same layer beyond a single protected boss contact. Tier Rushing Guide Run Sequence closes that defensive ladder with Second Wind after normal shield charges are gone. The guide is explicit that eHP Guide Round Triage still matters at the very start because if the tower can tank the first boss normally, the remaining one-time layers can be saved for later waves where the rush actually needs them.
interaction_summary: Tier Rushing begins with passive survivability if possible, then spends layered boss protections in order: Death Defy rolls first, Energy Shield plus Plasma Cannon buys clean boss kills, and Second Wind is the once-per-rush buffer that extends the sequence after shield charges are gone.

topic: Tier Rushing Guide Run Sequence with Missile Barrage, Missile Amplifier, Demon Mode, Nuke, and Milestones
title: Tier Rushing Guide Run Sequence with Missile Barrage, Missile Amplifier, Demon Mode, Nuke, and Milestones
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Tier Rushing manual finishers and their unlock or support systems, not the individual mechanics. It is not a Smart Missiles build guide or a card unlock table.
content: Tier Rushing Guide Run Sequence with Missile Barrage, Missile Amplifier, Demon Mode, Nuke, and Milestones. Tier Rushing Guide Run Sequence uses Missile Barrage as the first manual boss answer because it can preserve an Energy Shield charge on an early boss wave instead of spending one of the more limited defensive layers immediately. Missile Amplifier matters to that same route because the raw guide only recommends Missile Barrage confidently when the missile shell is strong enough to finish the boss instead of partially softening it. The guide still treats Missile Barrage as an unlocked option, not as a baseline requirement, because Milestones and labs gate when it exists at all. Demon Mode and Nuke come later in the sequence for different reasons. Demon Mode is the manual invulnerability bridge once Intro Sprint is already off, while Nuke is intentionally saved as the final forgiving boss cleanup tool after the rest of the rush shell has already been spent.
interaction_summary: Tier Rushing spends manual boss-kill tools only after earlier passive layers are gone: Missile Barrage is the first manual save if unlocked, Demon Mode is the long invulnerability bridge after Intro Sprint ends, and Nuke is the final forgiving cleanup tool once the other layers have already been committed.

topic: Tier Rushing Guide Timing Control and Run Sequence with Intro Sprint, Wave Accelerator, Slow Aura, Chrono Field, Demon Mode, and Second Wind
title: Tier Rushing Guide Timing Control and Run Sequence with Intro Sprint, Wave Accelerator, Slow Aura, Chrono Field, Demon Mode, and Second Wind
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Tier Rushing timing control and its duration-based tools, not the individual mechanics. It is not a generic crowd-control guide or a Chrono Field upgrade page.
content: Tier Rushing Guide Timing Control and Run Sequence with Intro Sprint, Wave Accelerator, Slow Aura, Chrono Field, Demon Mode, and Second Wind. Tier Rushing Guide Timing Control treats Intro Sprint as a retry-speed tool first and a reach-extension tool second. It gets the run back to the breakpoint quickly, and if the card is strong enough it can also let Second Wind span into a second boss wave before the rush shell is spent. Wave Accelerator works on that same timing problem by shortening the gap between waves. The guide uses it only when that timing compression helps Second Wind or Demon Mode touch an extra boss instead of leaving their duration partly wasted between waves. Slow Aura and Chrono Field are not just generic slows here. Tier Rushing Guide Timing Control uses them as boss-position tools so the player can delay one boss hit for Second Wind or Demon Mode, then release the next boss faster by turning the slow off before the following wave arrives. Tier Rushing Guide Run Sequence depends on that timing control because the whole rush order only works if those one-time layers are spent on the boss hits that matter most.
interaction_summary: Tier Rushing gets value from manipulating when bosses arrive, not just whether they die: Intro Sprint compresses retries, Wave Accelerator can stretch one invulnerability card across two boss waves, and Slow Aura or Chrono Field are used as timing levers so Second Wind and Demon Mode land on the boss hits that matter most.

topic: Tier Rushing Guide Overview and Breakpoints and Limits with Milestone Tier Progression, Tier Unlock Requirement, Tier Battle Conditions, Plasma Cannon, and Thorns
title: Tier Rushing Guide Overview and Breakpoints and Limits with Milestone Tier Progression, Tier Unlock Requirement, Tier Battle Conditions, Plasma Cannon, and Thorns
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Tier Rushing progression goals and its hard tier breakpoints, not the individual mechanics. It is not a generic tier ladder summary or a full battle-condition explainer.
content: Tier Rushing Guide Overview and Breakpoints and Limits with Milestone Tier Progression, Tier Unlock Requirement, Tier Battle Conditions, Plasma Cannon, and Thorns. Tier Rushing Guide Overview frames the strategy as a short-range unlock tactic, not a farming build. Milestone Tier Progression and Tier Unlock Requirement are the real reason it exists: early tiers are opened by wave-100 clears, so a run that only survives a few extra bosses can still unlock the next tier and its milestone table. That same short-range logic is why the guide says the strategy is mostly worthless far past wave 100. Once the rush shell has spent its one-time layers, the build does not have a real long-run economy or survivability engine behind it. Tier Rushing Guide Breakpoints and Limits makes Tier 14 the main failure point because Tier Battle Conditions start applying fixed resistance packages there. Plasma Cannon and Thorns are both hit by that change, so the classic Plasma Cannon plus Thorns boss finish becomes much less reliable exactly where the guide says the strategy stops being worth building around.
mechanics: Tier Rushing Guide Breakpoints and Limits
interaction_summary: Tier Rushing exists to clear early tier-unlock waves quickly, but it stops scaling once tier conditions start directly reducing the boss-kill shell. The guide therefore treats wave-100 milestone progression as the main target and marks Tier 14 as the point where Plasma Cannon and Thorns lose too much reliability under battle-condition resistance.

topic: Orbless Guide Overview with Spotlight, Golden Tower, Black Hole, Spotlight Coin Bonus, and Black Hole Coin Bonus
title: Orbless Guide Overview with Spotlight, Golden Tower, Black Hole, Spotlight Coin Bonus, and Black Hole Coin Bonus
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Orbless Guide Overview and its core overlapping multiplier systems, not the individual mechanics. It is not a generic Ultimate Weapon overview or a one-weapon upgrade plan.
content: Orbless Guide Overview with Spotlight, Golden Tower, Black Hole, Spotlight Coin Bonus, and Black Hole Coin Bonus. Orbless is built around overlap, not raw damage. Spotlight marks the preferred kill zone while Golden Tower and Black Hole provide the economy window that makes those localized kills worth more than general clearing. Spotlight Coin Bonus and Black Hole Coin Bonus both matter because each one scales kills made inside its own zone, so the guide is really trying to maximize the count of enemies that die while all three systems are lined up at once. That is why the guide treats spillage as the enemy: every kill outside the overlapping Spotlight, Golden Tower, and Black Hole window is a kill that spent enemy density without collecting the full multiplier stack.
interaction_summary: Orbless stacks Spotlight, Golden Tower, and Black Hole coin windows by concentrating kills inside the overlapping zone, then relies on Spotlight Coin Bonus and Black Hole Coin Bonus to multiply those localized kills instead of accepting broader screen-wide clears.

interaction_summary: The eHP card shell uses Health and Extra Defense to tank, Extra Orb and Attack Speed to control normal waves, Plasma Cannon to reduce boss-hit requirements, and Damage plus Berzerker to stop protectors from stalling the run, while Energy Net is avoided because it can worsen crowd-control timing.

Chrono Field is pushed later because it is expensive but powerful, and Wormhole Redirector fits the same late-support theme by adding another strong survivability layer once modules are available.
interaction_summary: The eHP guide treats Spotlight, Black Hole, and Death Wave as immediate support weapons, keeps Chrono Field as a later transition investment, and pairs that survivability arc well with Wormhole Redirector once module support exists.

interaction_summary: The eHP guide diagnoses failures by separating boss one-shots, repeated boss chains, normal-wave crowd-control leaks, protector stalls, and elite pressure such as vampires into different upgrade responses.

Early accounts use Defense Absolute and then Health because they need a cheap way to survive the first real devo tiers. Later, Defense %, Enemy Attack Level Skip, Wall Health, Wall Regen, and Wall Fortification become more important because the build is no longer dying to one simple damage source. Wormhole Redirector fits that later stage especially well because the guide treats Regen as weak early but very strong once the tower has enough supporting stats and module scaling to make it real.
interaction_summary: The Orb Devo survival ladder starts with Defense Absolute and Health on young accounts, then shifts into Defense %, Enemy Attack Level Skip, Wall scaling, and Wormhole Redirector-style Regen support as the account gains module depth.

content: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Overview with Ultimate Weapons and Power Stones. Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Overview is built on permanence. Ultimate Weapons cost Power Stones, later selections are more expensive than earlier ones, and each weak early choice delays a future pick that may have created stronger sync or farm value instead. That is why the guide ranks the whole Ultimate Weapons roster instead of judging each weapon only by its first unlocked state. Golden Tower, Black Hole, and Death Wave rise because their overlap value starts compounding earlier than the later damage or control specialists. The guide is therefore a strategic ordering layer for Ultimate Weapons and Power Stone spending, not a standalone stat description for one weapon at a time.
mechanics: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Overview
interaction_summary: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Overview exists because Ultimate Weapons are permanent Power Stone purchases whose opportunity cost compounds over time. The guide therefore ranks the roster around long-term economy, sync value, and support requirements rather than around isolated first-impression strength.

topic: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Economy Core with Golden Tower, Black Hole, Death Wave, Golden Tower Bonus, Black Hole Damage, Black Hole Coin Bonus, Death Wave Health, Death Wave Coins Bonus, Death Wave Cell Bonus, and Multiverse Nexus
title: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Economy Core with Golden Tower, Black Hole, Death Wave, Golden Tower Bonus, Black Hole Damage, Black Hole Coin Bonus, Death Wave Health, Death Wave Coins Bonus, Death Wave Cell Bonus, and Multiverse Nexus
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between the early UW economy shell and the lab or sync systems that make it scale, not the individual mechanics in isolation.
content: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Economy Core with Golden Tower, Black Hole, Death Wave, Golden Tower Bonus, Black Hole Damage, Black Hole Coin Bonus, Death Wave Health, Death Wave Coins Bonus, Death Wave Cell Bonus, and Multiverse Nexus. Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Economy Core treats Golden Tower as the first purchase because its value is immediate, then puts Black Hole second because current site data shows Black Hole Coin Bonus and Black Hole Damage unlocking a much stronger economy-and-protector shell once the labs are online. Death Wave stays in that same early group because its reward package is broader than raw damage. The guide specifically values coins, health, and cells arriving on hit, and current site data confirms Death Wave Health, Death Wave Coins Bonus, and Death Wave Cell Bonus as real progression levers that keep paying even after clean one-shots stop being normal. Multiverse Nexus fits this shell as a temporary sync aid rather than a permanent excuse to ignore natural timing. It can line up Golden Tower, Black Hole, and Death Wave earlier, but the guide still ranks those weapons highly because the shared economy window is the real prize, not the module by itself.
mechanics: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Economy Core
interaction_summary: The guide front-loads Golden Tower, Black Hole, and Death Wave because they create the strongest early economy shell once their labs and timing overlap are developed. Golden Tower starts the income engine immediately, Black Hole adds both coin and protector-clearing value, Death Wave adds coins, health, and cells on hit, and Multiverse Nexus can temporarily force shared timing while natural sync is still being built.

title: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Damage and Coin Follow-Ups with Spotlight, Spotlight Coin Bonus, Spotlight Missiles, Smart Missiles, Missile Amplifier, and Missile Radius
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between the mid-rank damage follow-up picks and their support systems, not any one weapon or lab alone.
content: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Damage and Coin Follow-Ups with Spotlight, Spotlight Coin Bonus, Spotlight Missiles, Smart Missiles, Missile Amplifier, and Missile Radius. Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Damage and Coin Follow-Ups puts Spotlight first because it solves two problems at once: Spotlight Coin Bonus adds another farming multiplier, and the base Spotlight bonus improves non-percent-health damage without needing a pure damage account on day one. Spotlight Missiles is the bridge between that early value and later missile builds. It gives Spotlight a real offensive lab shell before Smart Missiles is fully mature, which is why the raw guide still likes Spotlight as the fourth pick even when damage is not yet the tower main focus. Smart Missiles stays later because Missile Amplifier and Missile Radius are what convert it from a theoretical endgame weapon into a practical one. The guide therefore treats Spotlight as the earlier follow-up and Smart Missiles as the expensive ceiling that Spotlight eventually supports.
mechanics: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Damage and Coin Follow-Ups
interaction_summary: Spotlight comes before Smart Missiles because it adds both another coin multiplier and a broad damage-taken bonus with less setup. Smart Missiles eventually becomes the larger damage ceiling, but its real payoff depends on missile labs and on Spotlight-derived kill windows that are already mature.

title: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Control and Midgame Damage with Chrono Field, Chrono Field Duration, Chain Lightning, Chain Lightning Shock, Shock Chance, Shock Multiplier, and Dimension Core
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between the control pivot of the UW guide and the lab or module systems behind it, not the individual mechanics alone.
content: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Control and Midgame Damage with Chrono Field, Chrono Field Duration, Chain Lightning, Chain Lightning Shock, Shock Chance, Shock Multiplier, and Dimension Core. Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Control and Midgame Damage treats Chrono Field as the real control milestone because current site data confirms that Chrono Field Duration can push the weapon toward permanent uptime, which dramatically changes survival and enemy pacing. That same section makes the ranking conditional instead of rigid. If the account cannot keep a 3x lab boost running, Chrono Field should be taken earlier so the long duration grind starts sooner; if lab acceleration is already strong, Chain Lightning can move ahead because its useful damage spike arrives faster. Chain Lightning fills that bridge role through Chain Lightning Shock, Shock Chance, and Shock Multiplier, while Dimension Core turns the same package into a much stronger damage engine by expanding Shock stacking and doubling the key Shock stats.
mechanics: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Control and Midgame Damage
interaction_summary: Chrono Field is the guide’s main crowd-control pivot because duration investment can make it effectively permanent, while Chain Lightning is the cheaper midgame damage bridge that helps with elites during that buildout. The guide’s 5th-pick timing changes according to lab-boost capacity because Chrono Field Duration is a grind, and Dimension Core amplifies Chain Lightning’s Shock package once the account is ready for more damage.

topic: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Late-Game Specialists with Smart Missiles, Inner Land Mines, Inner Mine Stun, Magnetic Hook, Space Displacer, Poison Swamp, Swamp Radius, Poison Swamp Stun, Chrono Field, and Chrono Loop
title: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Late-Game Specialists with Smart Missiles, Inner Land Mines, Inner Mine Stun, Magnetic Hook, Space Displacer, Poison Swamp, Swamp Radius, Poison Swamp Stun, Chrono Field, and Chrono Loop
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between the late specialist picks in the UW guide and their support systems, not the individual mechanics or module pages in isolation.
content: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Late-Game Specialists with Smart Missiles, Inner Land Mines, Inner Mine Stun, Magnetic Hook, Space Displacer, Poison Swamp, Swamp Radius, Poison Swamp Stun, Chrono Field, and Chrono Loop. Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Late-Game Specialists puts Smart Missiles ahead of the final two weapons because it still becomes the main late-game damage engine once its lab shell is funded, even though it arrives later than Spotlight and Chain Lightning in practical account growth. Inner Land Mines is ranked near the bottom for timing reasons, not because the weapon is useless. Inner Mine Stun, Magnetic Hook, and Space Displacer all reinforce the same idea from the raw guide: ILM is strongest as a boss-and-elite control specialist once the account can support how those mines actually connect and hold targets in place, even though it is comparatively cheap to upgrade into visible impact. Poison Swamp remains the final recommendation because its payoff depends on enemies staying controlled long enough for the damage profile to ramp. Swamp Radius and Poison Swamp Stun are the first shell, but the raw guide is explicit that Poison Swamp is better after Chrono Field and preferably Chrono Loop support already exist, not before.
mechanics: Ultimate Weapon Pick Order Guide Late-Game Specialists
interaction_summary: The guide leaves Smart Missiles, Inner Land Mines, and Poison Swamp for later because each one needs a support shell before its real value appears. Smart Missiles wants mature missile scaling, Inner Land Mines wants stun or module delivery support, and Poison Swamp wants Chrono Field-level control depth so the ramping damage profile can actually matter.

title: Guilds Overview
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guilds mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guilds Overview. This file reorganizes guild and guardian knowledge into the same keyed mechanic format used by other deterministic knowledge sources. The original raw source remains preserved in public/knowledge/guilds for side-by-side comparison. Definition: Guilds are a seasonal social progression system that grants shared participation rewards, guild-shop access, and guardians. Type: System. Domain: Social Progression. Section: Guilds. Category: Social. Behavior: Guilds unlock at Milestone Tier 3 Wave 10. Players can join an existing guild or create their own guild. Each guild supports up to 30 players. Joining a guild opens guild rewards, guild-shop purchases, and guardians.

title: Guild Creation
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guild Creation mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guild Creation. Definition: Guild Creation lets a player found a new guild with its own setup and join rules. Type: Access Rule. Domain: Guilds. Section: Guilds. Category: Membership. Aliases: create guild. Behavior: Creating a guild costs 50 gems. The creator chooses the guild name, description, and icon. Join policy can be Free, With Approval, or Invitation Only.

title: Guild Joining
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guild Joining mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guild Joining. Definition: Guild Joining is the process of finding a guild and entering it under that guild's join rules. Type: Access Rule. Domain: Guilds. Section: Guilds. Category: Membership. Aliases: join guild. Behavior: Players can search the available guild list and request to join shown guilds. Free guilds allow immediate entry. With Approval guilds require leader approval. Invitation Only guilds do not appear in the public guild list.

title: Guild Rewards
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guild Rewards mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guild Rewards. Definition: Guild Rewards are the recurring resource payouts and unlocks tied to guild participation. Type: Reward System. Domain: Guilds. Section: Guilds. Category: Rewards. Aliases: guild reward rules. Behavior: Joining a guild gives access to guardians. Guild contribution is earned from Weekly Challenge boxes. Coin reward scales from the player's highest unlocked tier. Players can reference Daily Missions to see their base coin reward.

title: Guild Contribution
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guild Contribution mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guild Contribution. Definition: Guild Contribution is the weekly participation total used to unlock guild reward chests. Type: Progress Metric. Domain: Guilds. Section: Guilds. Category: Rewards. Aliases: contribution. Behavior: Guild contribution is earned from Weekly Challenge boxes. Weekly reward chest breakpoints are 100, 250, 500, and 750 contribution. Higher contribution unlocks more tokens, bits, coins, and gems.

title: Guild Weekly Reward Chests
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guild Weekly Reward Chests mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guild Weekly Reward Chests. Definition: Guild Weekly Reward Chests are the four contribution-based payout tiers for guild participation. Type: Reward Table. Domain: Guilds. Section: Guilds. Category: Rewards. Aliases: weekly guild chests; guild chest rewards. Behavior: 100 contribution gives 10 tokens, 10 bits, 1x coins, and 5 gems. 250 contribution gives 20 tokens, 25 bits, 2x coins, and 10 gems. 500 contribution gives 40 tokens, 50 bits, 3x coins, and 15 gems. 750 contribution gives 80 tokens, 100 bits, 5x coins, and 30 gems. Claiming all four chests totals 150 tokens, 185 bits, 11x coins, and 60 gems.

title: Guild Seasons
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guild Seasons mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guild Seasons. Definition: Guild Seasons are the repeating time window that controls guild shops, guild themes, and token carryover. Type: Seasonal Rule. Domain: Guilds. Section: Guilds. Category: Seasons. Aliases: guild season. Behavior: Each guild season lasts 8 weeks. Guild-shop purchase ladders reset at the beginning of the next season. Guild themes rotate by season and can be missed. Unused guild tokens are resolved through guild token cashout when the season ends.

title: Guild Token Cashout
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guild Token Cashout mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guild Token Cashout. Definition: Guild Token Cashout converts leftover guild tokens into gems automatically when a guild season ends. Type: Conversion Rule. Domain: Guilds. Section: Guilds. Category: Seasons. Aliases: token cashout; token conversion. Behavior: Unspent guild tokens convert to gems at a 5 to 1 ratio. The result rounds up to the next whole gem. Five guild tokens become one gem. Cashout happens automatically at the end of each 8-week guild season.

title: Guild Shop
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guild Shop mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guild Shop. Definition: Guild Shop is the seasonal store that spends guild tokens on currencies, cosmetics, relics, and guardian-chip unlocks. Type: Store. Domain: Guilds. Section: Guilds. Category: Purchases. Aliases: guild store. Behavior: Guild shop purchases spend guild tokens. The shop offers currencies, themes, relics, and chips. Currency purchase ladders reset at the start of the next guild season.

title: Guild Shop Currency Purchases
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guild Shop Currency Purchases mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guild Shop Currency Purchases. Definition: Guild Shop Currency Purchases are the seasonal token ladders for bits, gems, and shards. Type: Cost Ladder. Domain: Guild Tokens. Section: Guilds. Category: Purchases. Aliases: guild currency costs; guild shop costs. Behavior: Currencies available are bits, gems, and shards. Guild-token exchange gives 100 gems or 250 shards. There are four shard types, and only the purchased shard type increases in cost. Each listed currency purchase is capped at three buys per season. Costs: Bits cost 25, 50, and 75 tokens for purchases one through three. Gems cost 15, 25, and 40 tokens for purchases one through three. Shards cost 5, 10, and 15 tokens for purchases one through three.

title: Guild Themes
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guild Themes mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guild Themes. Definition: Guild Themes are seasonal cosmetic purchases sold in the guild shop and kept permanently once bought. Type: Cosmetic Rotation. Domain: Guilds. Section: Guilds. Category: Purchases. Aliases: guild skins; seasonal themes. Behavior: Themes rotate every guild season and may be missed. One tower theme costs 100 tokens. One background theme costs 100 tokens. One menu theme costs 100 tokens. One guardian skin costs 150 tokens. Purchased themes remain available forever.

title: Guild Relics
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guild Relics mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guild Relics. Definition: Guild Relics are limited relic purchases sold through the guild shop at seasonal token price points. Type: Limited Purchase. Domain: Guilds. Section: Guilds. Category: Purchases. Aliases: guild relics. Behavior: Guild relics are sold at 75-token and 150-token price points. Guild relics may be limited to the event that sponsors them. Guild relic offers can be seasonal or time-limited.

title: Guardians Overview
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guardians mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guardians Overview. Definition: Guardians are temporary-bonus guild companions with upgradeable chip stats and unlockable chip slots. Type: Companion System. Domain: Guilds. Section: Guilds. Category: Guardians. Aliases: guardian system. Behavior: Joining a guild gives access to guardians. Guardians are similar to bots and provide temporary bonuses while active. Guardian chip slots can be unlocked up to four total. Guardian chip upgrades cost bits.

title: Guardian Chips
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Guardian Chips mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, implementation details, or other game systems.
content: Guardian Chips. Definition: Guardian Chips are the guardian abilities and upgrade lines that define each guardian's effect, cooldown, and secondary stat. Type: Upgrade System. Domain: Guardians. Section: Guilds. Category: Guardians. Aliases: guardian upgrades; guardian chips. Behavior: Ally and Attack unlock when guardians unlock. Bounty, Fetch, Scout, and Summon are purchased in the guild shop for 200 tokens each. Guardian chip upgrades cost bits. Each guardian has three core upgrade stats with separate level caps and cost ladders.

topic: Guild Rewards with Guild Contribution and Guild Weekly Reward Chests
title: Guild Rewards with Guild Contribution and Guild Weekly Reward Chests
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Guild Rewards, Guild Contribution, and Guild Weekly Reward Chests, not the individual mechanics. It is not about guild creation, guardian upgrade costs, or unrelated reward systems.
content: Guild Rewards with Guild Contribution and Guild Weekly Reward Chests. Guild Contribution is the weekly participation score that determines which Guild Weekly Reward Chests can be claimed. Those Guild Weekly Reward Chests are the main recurring Guild Rewards source for tokens, bits, coins, and gems. This means Guild Rewards scale with how much Guild Contribution a player earns during the weekly cycle.
interaction_summary: Guild Contribution unlocks Guild Weekly Reward Chests, and those chests are how most recurring Guild Rewards are paid out.

topic: Guild Seasons with Guild Token Cashout and Gems
title: Guild Seasons with Guild Token Cashout and Gems
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Guild Seasons, Guild Token Cashout, and Gems, not the individual mechanics. It is not about guardian chip costs, guild joining rules, or unrelated currencies.
content: Guild Seasons with Guild Token Cashout and Gems. Guild Seasons last eight weeks and define when seasonal reset behavior happens. At the end of that season, Guild Token Cashout automatically converts leftover guild tokens into Gems at a rounded-up 5 to 1 ratio. Because of that timing, Guild Seasons determine when unused guild-token value turns into Gems instead of remaining shop currency.
interaction_summary: Guild Seasons define when Guild Token Cashout occurs, and Guild Token Cashout converts leftover guild tokens into Gems.

topic: Guild Shop with Guild Shop Currency Purchases and Guild Tokens
title: Guild Shop with Guild Shop Currency Purchases and Guild Tokens
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Guild Shop, Guild Shop Currency Purchases, and Guild Tokens, not the individual mechanics. It is not about relic tracker implementation, weekly chest thresholds, or unrelated currencies.
content: Guild Shop with Guild Shop Currency Purchases and Guild Tokens. Guild Tokens are the currency consumed by the Guild Shop. Guild Shop Currency Purchases define how many Guild Tokens each seasonal purchase of bits, gems, or shards requires. This means the live value of Guild Tokens depends on which step of each Guild Shop Currency Purchases ladder the player is currently on.
interaction_summary: Guild Shop spends Guild Tokens, and Guild Shop Currency Purchases define the seasonal token ladders for bits, gems, and shards.

topic: Guild Themes with Guild Seasons and Guild Shop
title: Guild Themes with Guild Seasons and Guild Shop
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Guild Themes, Guild Seasons, and Guild Shop, not the individual mechanics. It is not about relic rarity, guardian chip costs, or unrelated cosmetic systems.
content: Guild Themes with Guild Seasons and Guild Shop. Guild Themes are purchased from the Guild Shop rather than earned through weekly chest thresholds. Guild Seasons rotate which tower, background, menu, and guardian-skin options are currently available in that shop. As a result, Guild Themes availability depends on both the Guild Shop and the active Guild Seasons rotation window.
interaction_summary: Guild Themes are sold through the Guild Shop, and Guild Seasons control which theme rotation is currently available.

topic: Guild Relics with Guild Seasons and Guild Shop
title: Guild Relics with Guild Seasons and Guild Shop
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Guild Relics, Guild Seasons, and Guild Shop, not the individual mechanics. It is not about weekly reward tables, guardian stat caps, or unrelated relic systems.
content: Guild Relics with Guild Seasons and Guild Shop. Guild Relics are purchased from the Guild Shop at fixed seasonal token price points. Because Guild Relics can be limited or event-tied, Guild Seasons influence which relic offers appear in the shop rotation. This makes Guild Relics availability a combined result of Guild Shop inventory and the current Guild Seasons window.
interaction_summary: Guild Relics appear through the Guild Shop, and Guild Seasons influence which limited relic offers are available at a given time.

topic: Guardians with Guilds and Guild Rewards
title: Guardians with Guilds and Guild Rewards
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Guardians, Guilds, and Guild Rewards, not the individual mechanics. It is not about bot formulas, module assists, or unrelated progression systems.
content: Guardians with Guilds and Guild Rewards. Guardians are unlocked only after the player is participating in Guilds. Guild Rewards provide the token and bit economy that makes ongoing guardian progression possible after that unlock. This means Guardians are not a standalone system; they sit downstream of Guilds access and recurring Guild Rewards income.
interaction_summary: Guardians only exist inside Guilds, and Guild Rewards progression is what opens and funds most guardian progression.

topic: Guardian Chips with Bits and Guardians
title: Guardian Chips with Bits and Guardians
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Guardian Chips, Bits, and Guardians, not the individual mechanics. It is not about guild creation cost, relic purchases, or unrelated currencies.
content: Guardian Chips with Bits and Guardians. Guardian Chips hold the effect, cooldown, and secondary-stat upgrade lines for each guardian. Bits are the upgrade currency consumed when those guardian chip lines are leveled. Because each guardian stat has its own cap and bit-cost ladder, Guardians progress through Guardian Chips only as Bits are invested into those specific lines.
interaction_summary: Guardian Chips define each guardian upgrade line, and Bits are the resource spent to raise those guardian chip stats.

topic: Guardian Chips with Guild Shop and Guild Tokens
title: Guardian Chips with Guild Shop and Guild Tokens
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Guardian Chips, Guild Shop, and Guild Tokens, not the individual mechanics. It is not about weekly chest coin multipliers, relic pricing, or unrelated reward systems.
content: Guardian Chips with Guild Shop and Guild Tokens. Ally and Attack are the only Guardian Chips that start unlocked with the guardian system itself. Bounty, Fetch, Scout, and Summon must be purchased separately from the Guild Shop for Guild Tokens. This makes Guild Shop access and Guild Tokens the gate on expanding Guardian Chips beyond the two default guardian abilities.
interaction_summary: Extra Guardian Chips are bought through the Guild Shop, and Guild Tokens pay the unlock cost for those additional guardian abilities.

title: Attack Guardian
disambiguation: This chunk is about Attack Guardian as a guardian mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated guild rules, other guardians, or tracker implementation details.
content: Attack Guardian. Definition: Attack Guardian attacks nearby enemies and deals damage equal to a percentage of the damage they have already taken. Type: Guardian Chip. Domain: Guardians. Section: Guilds. Category: Guardian. Aliases: Attack. Behavior: Its three upgrade stats are Percentage, Cooldown, and Targets. Base values are Percentage 1%, Cooldown 120s, and Targets 1. Higher levels raise Percentage, reduce Cooldown, and increase Targets until each stat reaches its own cap. Guardian stats: Percentage, Cooldown, Targets. Percentage ranges from 1% at L0 to 20% at L19. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 25 bits at L1 to 475 bits at L19. Cooldown ranges from 120s at L0 to 30s at L89. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 1 bits at L1 to 90 bits at L89. Targets ranges from 1 at L0 to 10 at L9. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 100 bits at L1 to 900 bits at L9. Attack Guardian does not cap all three stats at the same level, so some upgrade lines stop improving before others.

title: Ally Guardian
disambiguation: This chunk is about Ally Guardian as a guardian mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated guild rules, other guardians, or tracker implementation details.
content: Ally Guardian. Definition: Ally Guardian converts an enemy into an ally recovery package that can heal the tower beyond basic maximum recovery. Type: Guardian Chip. Domain: Guardians. Section: Guilds. Category: Guardian. Aliases: Ally. Behavior: Its three upgrade stats are Recovery Amount, Max Recovery, and Cooldown. Base values are Recovery Amount 1%, Max Recovery x1.1, and Cooldown 120s. Higher levels increase healing values and reduce Cooldown until each stat reaches its own cap. Guardian stats: Recovery Amount, Max Recovery, Cooldown. Recovery Amount ranges from 1% at L0 to 25% at L24. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 10 bits at L1 to 125 bits at L24. Max Recovery ranges from x1.1 at L0 to x6.0 at L49. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 1 bits at L1 to 49 bits at L49. Cooldown ranges from 120s at L0 to 30s at L89. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 1 bits at L1 to 90 bits at L89. Ally Guardian does not cap all three stats at the same level, so some upgrade lines stop improving before others.

title: Bounty Guardian
disambiguation: This chunk is about Bounty Guardian as a guardian mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated guild rules, other guardians, or tracker implementation details.
content: Bounty Guardian. Definition: Bounty Guardian places a bounty on nearby non-common enemies so they grant more coins on death. Type: Guardian Chip. Domain: Guardians. Section: Guilds. Category: Guardian. Aliases: Bounty. Behavior: Its three upgrade stats are Multiplier, Cooldown, and Targets. Base values are Multiplier x0.01, Cooldown 120s, and Targets 1. Higher levels raise Multiplier, reduce Cooldown, and increase Targets until each stat reaches its own cap. Guardian stats: Multiplier, Cooldown, Targets. Multiplier ranges from x0.01 at L0 to x1.00 at L99. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 1 bits at L1 to 99 bits at L99. Cooldown ranges from 120s at L0 to 60s at L60. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 2 bits at L1 to 120 bits at L60. Targets ranges from 1 at L0 to 10 at L9. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 100 bits at L1 to 900 bits at L9. Bounty Guardian does not cap all three stats at the same level, so some upgrade lines stop improving before others.

title: Fetch Guardian
disambiguation: This chunk is about Fetch Guardian as a guardian mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated guild rules, other guardians, or tracker implementation details.
content: Fetch Guardian. Definition: Fetch Guardian locates and retrieves hidden loot such as coins, gems, medals, shards, and modules. Type: Guardian Chip. Domain: Guardians. Section: Guilds. Category: Guardian. Aliases: Fetch. Behavior: Its three upgrade stats are Cooldown, Find Chance, and Double Find Chance. Base values are Cooldown 120s, Find Chance 10%, and Double Find Chance 2%. Higher levels reduce Cooldown and improve both loot-find stats until each stat reaches its own cap. Guardian stats: Cooldown, Find Chance, Double Find Chance. Cooldown ranges from 120s at L0 to 61s at L59. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 2 bits at L1 to 118 bits at L59. Find Chance ranges from 10% at L0 to 50% at L40. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 20 bits at L1 to 215 bits at L40. Double Find Chance ranges from 2% at L0 to 50% at L48. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 10 bits at L1 to 245 bits at L48. Fetch Guardian does not cap all three stats at the same level, so some upgrade lines stop improving before others.

title: Scout Guardian
disambiguation: This chunk is about Scout Guardian as a guardian mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated guild rules, other guardians, or tracker implementation details.
content: Scout Guardian. Definition: Scout Guardian treats enemies as being farther from the tower for damage calculations while the guardian is active. Type: Guardian Chip. Domain: Guardians. Section: Guilds. Category: Guardian. Aliases: Scout. Behavior: Its three upgrade stats are Cooldown, Range Bonus, and Duration. Base values are Cooldown 105s, Range Bonus x2.0, and Duration 5s. Scout Guardian was introduced in Guild Season 7. Higher levels reduce Cooldown and increase both Range Bonus and Duration until each stat reaches its own cap. Guardian stats: Cooldown, Range Bonus, Duration. Cooldown ranges from 105s at L0 to 35s at L70. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 1 bits at L1 to 139 bits at L70. Range Bonus ranges from x2.0 at L0 to x6.0 at L40. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 10 bits at L1 to 205 bits at L40. Duration ranges from 5s at L0 to 35s at L30. Upgrade costs shown in site data run from 10 bits at L1 to 300 bits at L30. Scout Guardian does not cap all three stats at the same level, so some upgrade lines stop improving before others.

title: Lab Switching

content: Lab Switching. Definition: Lab Switching lets a player swap the active research to another lab. Type: Research Rule. Domain: Labs. Section: Labs. Category: Research Management. When that lab is resumed later, the coins must be paid again.

content: Lab Rushing. Definition: Lab Rushing skips the entire remaining lab time by spending Gems. Type: Time Skip. Domain: Gems. Section: Labs. Category: Time Acceleration. Longer lab times have built-in discounts, so Gem cost per unit time becomes cheaper on long researches. Gold boxing labs increases Gem rush efficiency, making rushing require fewer Gems.

title: Lab Boosting
disambiguation: This chunk is about the Lab Boosting mechanic itself, not its interactions. It is not about unrelated tracker state, other game systems, or implementation details.
content: Lab Boosting. Definition: Lab Boosting spends Elite Cells to temporarily accelerate research speed on active labs. Type: Time Acceleration. Domain: Elite Cells. Section: Labs. Category: Time Acceleration. Aliases: lab boosts; speed up labs. Behavior: Labs can be boosted to 1.5x, 2x, 3x, 4x, 5x, 6x, 7x, or 8x. Boost durations are 1 hour, 8 hours, or 24 hours. The player selects Speed Up, then a duration, then a multiplier, and the game shows the Elite Cell cost. Lab boosts use flat-rate costs by multiplier and duration since v25.5. Higher multipliers cost disproportionately more than the extra speed they provide, so spreading boosts across several labs is often more efficient than boosting one lab harder. Lab boosts can be configured to auto-queue when completed. Lab boosts only tick while a lab is slotted for research.

title: Lab Slots and Milestones
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Lab Slots and Milestones, not the individual mechanics. It is not about boost costs, rushing formulas, or unrelated research families.
content: Lab Slots and Milestones. Lab Slots begin only after the Milestones unlock at Tier 1 Wave 30. Milestones also gate many individual labs, so more Lab Slots do not bypass Milestones requirements by themselves. This means Milestones control when Lab Slots become useful and when those slots can be filled with more advanced labs.
interaction_summary: Milestones unlock the first Lab Slots access and gate many labs before those slots can research them.

title: Lab Rushing and Gems
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Lab Rushing and Gems, not the individual mechanics. It is not about Elite Cells boosts, slot purchases, or unrelated progression systems.
content: Lab Rushing and Gems. Lab Rushing consumes Gems to finish the whole remaining timer at once. Because Gem efficiency improves on longer timers, the Gem cost per unit time is better on long researches than on short ones. Gold boxing further improves the Gems side of Lab Rushing by lowering Gem cost for the same remaining time.
interaction_summary: Lab Rushing spends Gems to skip the entire remaining research time, with better gem efficiency on longer labs.

title: Lab Boosting and Elite Cells
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Lab Boosting and Elite Cells, not the individual mechanics. It is not about Gem rushing, slot unlocks, or unrelated currencies.
content: Lab Boosting and Elite Cells. Lab Boosting uses Elite Cells as its fuel for 1.5x through 8x research speed packages. Elite Cells costs are flat by multiplier and duration pair, but those Elite Cells costs rise far faster than the extra speed gained at the highest multipliers. This makes Elite Cells budgeting a major part of Lab Boosting decisions, especially when comparing one powerful boost against several lower boosts.
interaction_summary: Lab Boosting spends Elite Cells on flat-rate multiplier and duration packages, with high multipliers scaling in cost much faster than speed gained.

title: Lab Boosting and Slotted Research
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Lab Boosting and Slotted Research, not the individual mechanics. It is not about Gem rush pricing, slot purchases, or unrelated automation systems.
content: Lab Boosting and Slotted Research. Lab Boosting does not advance idle labs; it only ticks when that lab is actively slotted for research. This means Slotted Research status is the live gate on whether Lab Boosting is actually producing progress. If a lab is unslotted, the purchased Lab Boosting time exists but does not convert into research progress until the lab is slotted again.
interaction_summary: Lab Boosting only advances timers while the boosted lab remains actively slotted for research.

topic: Lab Switching with Coins and Research Progress
title: Lab Switching with Coins and Research Progress
disambiguation: This chunk is about the interaction between Lab Switching, Coins, and Research Progress, not the individual mechanics. It is not about boost costs, slot counts, or unrelated lab families.
content: Lab Switching with Coins and Research Progress. Lab Switching returns the currently spent Coins when the player swaps to another lab. Research Progress is preserved instead of erased, so the unfinished lab can be resumed later from its stored green time. When that saved Research Progress is resumed, Coins must be paid again before the lab continues.
interaction_summary: Lab Switching refunds Coins immediately but preserves Research Progress so the lab can resume later after Coins are paid again.

content: Damage Mastery with Damage. Damage Mastery is the lab-side progression path for the card mechanic Damage. Card Mastery Unlock is required before Damage Mastery can matter in practice, because Damage Mastery extends the mastery tied to Damage.
